note: Path cost heuristics or search-ordering functions can be evolved against a benchmark of the game's own maps for fewer node expansions at equal route quality, as FunSearch evolved priority functions.
Evolving solutions to each puzzle before launch estimates near-optimal cost, cycle or area scores, anchoring histogram axes and flagging degenerate puzzles.
Job-to-hauler assignment is a scheduling problem like the Borg case; the dispatch heuristic can be evolved against simulated throughput and idle time on recorded colony states.
Rivals or coaches could evolve programs in the game's own language against its evaluator, so player-written code competes with machine-evolved code under the same rules.
Utility scoring functions can be evolved as code against designer metrics (survival, need satisfaction, behavior variety), keeping the result readable unlike a neural policy.
Automatic load and stop-ordering heuristics resemble the bin-packing heuristics FunSearch improved, and can be evolved against delivery-rate benchmarks.
Agent pass rates plus a player-population model estimate how a difficulty ramp drives churn, so threat and difficulty curves can be tuned before release instead of from live telemetry.
Curiosity and RL agents explore traversal exhaustively, finding stuck spots, missing collision, and shortcuts that scripted navmesh bots do not reach.
Search agents measure how many actions each career path needs to reach each level, exposing careers that are much faster or slower than the rest, as in The Sims Mobile study.
Agents replaying the early game measure when resource and progression thresholds are reached, so unlock pacing is set from distributions instead of a few manual runs.
Each scenario or level gets a predicted pass rate from human-like agents, letting designers order and adjust goals and constraints against a target difficulty curve.
Agent playthroughs estimate win rates and dominant unit mixes in statistical combat before release.
Generated content extends from text, items, and levels to complete executable rule sets that are compiled and filtered by playability and balance tests before anyone plays them.
Laws players propose could be translated by a code model into enforceable rule code and run through the same compile and playout tests GAVEL uses, rejecting laws that fail to compile or break play.

Candidate policies can be written as rule code in the game's own description language and screened by agent playouts for dominance and balance, so a policy list can be grown by search rather than authored one law at a time.
End conditions are generated together with the rules and kept only if MCTS play reaches them without trivial draws or one-sided wins, replacing hand-tuned victory thresholds.
Self-play over each generated variant measures first-player advantage, decisiveness, and the share of states with real choices, so turn order, phases, and move allowances can be adjusted by search.

Diplomacy becomes free-text negotiation with AI factions that propose specific joint moves, commit to them, and change plans when persuaded, instead of accept or decline treaty menus driven by opinion scores.
Typed messages are translated into predicted intents that feed a planner, so what the player says changes what the AI does on the map, and the AI's replies are constrained to match its own plan.
Planner-grounded dialogue lets AI counterparties propose, counter, and keep terms in free text instead of accepting or rejecting fixed offers.

An AI that models what others expect it to do can also track whether the player's stated intentions matched their moves, turning standing into a learned estimate of trustworthiness rather than a scalar moved by scripted events.
Peace terms could be negotiated in language against the war score, with the planner checking what the opponent will actually accept.
Card prompts, two to four options, and per-meter effect values can be generated in the game's card schema with effect sizes bounded by the grammar, leaving designers to curate rather than write.

Generated items, recipes, or characters can be written straight into typed game state (enum types, bounded stats, existing ids) instead of shown as text or parsed with retries, because invalid records cannot be emitted.
Free player text can be mapped onto the closed set of verbs and target ids legal in the current state, so conversation reliably triggers real game actions rather than only replies.
Laws proposed in plain language can be compiled into the world's structured condition-and-effect rule language by grammar-constrained generation, so players need not learn the rule editor.

An LLM can be dropped into the action-selection slot by constraining it to choose among the same enumerated actions the utility scorer would rank, keeping the engine's action set and preconditions intact.
ASAL turns a text prompt into a search over simulation rules that produce the described phenomenon, a route to generating new creature rule sets from player or designer descriptions at design time.
In Flow-Lenia, rules travel with matter, so selection can act on creatures that emerge from the physics itself rather than on declared fitness stats.
Rule parameters mix where creatures meet in Flow-Lenia, giving inheritance and hybridization as a spatial process instead of an explicit genome crossover function.

For movement abilities such as grappling hooks, jetpacks, and double jumps, a learned policy replaces hand-placed navigation-mesh links, so NPCs can traverse spaces designers would otherwise annotate by hand.

Players practice against an opponent whose skill comes from the same controls and physics, at selectable levels (Beginner to Expert, then custom tire and fuel settings), raising the ceiling of a skill-centered mechanic.

AI drivers operate the same tire, suspension, and weight-transfer model as the player at champion level, so handling fidelity matters in races against the AI instead of being sidestepped by scripted racing lines.
GradABM shows transmission parameters of a million-agent outbreak model calibrated to real case data by gradients, a route to epidemic games whose curves match real diseases or designer targets.
The gradient of a design's rating with respect to each part parameter tells the player which strut, joint or track segment most changes the score, enabling hints like 'move this support left'.
Differentiable fluid kernels (Warp, DiffTaichi) allow inverse design, solving for emitter or vent settings that produce a target flow, usable for level authoring or tuning puzzles.
A controller for a player-built soft or articulated body can be optimized in tens of gradient iterations, so assembled machines can learn to walk or swim during play.
Material stiffness and damping of node-beam or finite-element bodies can be fitted to reference motion or a target feel by gradient descent, as DiffTaichi does for elastic objects.
Tire, suspension and drivetrain constants can be fitted to recorded telemetry by differentiating lap or trajectory error, replacing manual parameter sweeps.

Avatar movement, camera response, and weapon use are predicted frame by frame from keyboard and mouse input instead of computed by engine code; responsiveness depends on denoising steps and frame rate (20 fps GameNGen and Oasis, about 10 fps DIAMOND CS:GO).

Every frame, enemy, and pickup is generated content conditioned on play, so a game can in principle contain situations its source game never had; in practice output stays inside the training game's distribution.

Terrain is invented on demand from the learned distribution of the training game with no seed or noise function (Oasis), but it is not persistent: regions that leave the short context window are regenerated differently on return.
Collision, gravity, and jumping are learned statistically from pixels rather than integrated; rules the data rarely violates can still be broken, as with DIAMOND's repeated mid-air jumps in CS:GO.

In Oasis and MineWorld, breaking and placing Minecraft blocks is predicted as pixels with no stored voxel grid, so edits are not durable; Oasis placing a dirt block can bring up an entirely different environment.

Photoreal props and scenery can be captured from photos in under an hour of training instead of modeled and textured by hand, enlarging decor catalogs that beauty scores consume; lighting is baked into the capture.
PhysGaussian deforms captured objects with MPM directly on the rendered Gaussians, so a scanned real object can bend, dent, or flow without building a node-beam or finite-element mesh first.
The player can hand an avatar or task to an agent that pursues a stated goal in any game it can see, without game-specific AI code, and that explains what it intends to do.
SIMA 2 converses about its surroundings, answers questions about the scene, and explains its actions, grounding dialogue in what it sees on screen.
Agents that follow language instructions and watch play could learn routines from a single narrated demonstration instead of recorded literal steps.
Self-improving agents that advance through a game's tech tree can serve as automated playtesters of progression in builds they were not trained on.

A companion can take open-ended spoken or typed orders, sketches, or emoji and carry them out with ordinary game controls, so the command vocabulary is no longer limited to the verbs a designer bound to buttons.

Chisel turns a coarse blockout into a detailed styled scene, the same rough-input to detailed-output contract as Townscaper-style build assist but with a learned generator; today it is an editor mode, not a runtime player tool.

Maps come from a prompt, photo, or video rather than a seed and noise pipeline, and unlike frame-based world models the result is baked geometry that persists, can be saved, and can be expanded region by region.
Exported collider meshes give generated scenes collision geometry automatically; Marble describes them as coarse, so precise physics still needs cleanup.
Bespoke scenario maps can be produced from a reference image or description and exported with collider meshes, reducing hand modeling per scenario; objectives and rules still need authoring.

Because an agent's state is natural-language memories, plans, and reflections, the player or designer can read them directly or interview the agent about why it acted, which is how the original paper evaluated believability.
Wants generated from an agent's own memories and reflections rather than rolled from a fixed table tied to an aspiration.

Each agent writes its own day plan from its description and memories, decomposed into hour and 5-15 minute steps and revised on events, in place of authored routine tables; the player still sees rhythms of work, meals, and leisure.

Information moves through generated conversations whose content comes from memory retrieval, so what spreads, to whom, and how it is reworded emerge from dialogue; in Smallville party awareness rose from 4% to 52% of agents with 1.3% hallucinated answers.

Memories become free-text records with LLM-rated importance, retrieved by recency, importance, and relevance, plus reflections that summarize many records into beliefs, instead of a fixed catalog of timed mood modifiers.
Memory streams summarized at low frequency give off-screen characters histories that persist when the player returns.

Relationships are held as remembered interactions and reflections about another agent rather than a numeric affinity, so a relationship's state is a set of retrievable facts; Smallville's acquaintance network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74 in two days.
Agents open-endedly converse, invite, and coordinate (for example planning and attending a party) without a predefined catalog of social moves and preconditions.

The next action is chosen by prompting with the current plan step, perceived surroundings, and retrieved memories rather than by scoring options against need curves, so choices can reference past events and other agents.
First- or third-person character movement is rendered by the model from WASD, camera, and jump input; the action space is small and collisions are not guaranteed (characters passing through walls).
Whole explorable scenes, characters, and events are generated at runtime from player text, sketches, or photos, which extends generative content from text and items to playable space.

Promptable world events work as a free-form god power: typed text adds characters, objects, or weather to the running world; Genie 3 attaches no cost or rule to them and their effects exist only in rendered frames.

Worlds come from a text or image prompt instead of a seed and noise pipeline, in any visual style; persistence is minutes long (about one minute of visual memory in Genie 3, 60-second sessions in Project Genie).

Object responses such as doors opening, balloons bursting, water, and smoke are produced by learned video dynamics (Genie 2) rather than a physics engine, with no conservation or collision guarantees.

A director could inject an event (a new character, object, or condition) as a text prompt that Genie 3 renders into the running world, removing per-event art and animation; event selection and pacing still need a separate system with real state.

Genie 3's promptable world events change weather by text during a session with no weather simulation or authored weather assets; the change is visual only and has no stored state for crops, agents, or travel to read.
MeshGraphNets learned aerodynamic flow around airfoils, pointing to flight models driven by surrogate CFD fields instead of fixed lift and drag coefficient tables.
Learned fluid surrogates (GNS particles, FNO fields) reproduce solver-quality flow at large speedups, raising resolution or extent of water and gas within a frame budget.
Neural operators solve parametric flow PDEs in one forward pass at any grid resolution, a candidate replacement for per-cell iterative water-flow updates over large terrains.
GNS simulates several materials (fluids, rigid solids, deformables) interacting in one learned model, so mixed-material reactions need no hand-written pairwise rules.
MeshGraphNets predicts cloth and structural deformation 10-100x faster than its training solver, allowing finite-element-like deformation where games now use coarse node-beam models.
Learned structural-mechanics surrogates output stress and deformation fields, which could replace binary support checks with graded bending, sagging and stress-driven failure.
Segment-level response to advertising predicted from models of human choice instead of a flat awareness multiplier.
Visitor populations could be drawn from person-grounded profiles whose preferences and tolerances are measured against real people rather than sampled from designer distributions.

Customer purchase decisions could be sampled from a model trained on human choice data, giving realistic heterogeneity and biases, instead of utility = value x preference - price with hand-set weights.
Before ship, designers could estimate option pick rates for each card by querying a choice model on the card text; untested on game content.
Simulated electorates could be built from survey-grounded agents that reproduce subgroup opinion distributions, so vote shares respond to issues the way measured populations do.
A group's preferences over policies could be derived from simulated members (silicon samples) rather than a single authored ideology vector.
Counterparties whose acceptance follows models of human bargaining (fairness, anchoring) rather than a single reservation price.
A character's disposition can be a rich text profile whose predicted Big Five scores and economic-game behavior match a real respondent, rather than a few discrete trait tags.
Mode-choice weights for time, cost, and comfort can be fitted to predicted human choices instead of hand-set.
AI bidders play mixed strategies over private valuations instead of bidding a fixed fraction of value, which removes simple exploits such as always outbidding the AI by one unit.

AI players reason over unseen state as a belief distribution and play strategies that are hard to exploit, instead of cheating with full map knowledge or ignoring hidden units, so concealment and feints work against the AI as they would against a person.

Deception becomes a stable part of AI play, as DeepNash bluffed with hidden unit identities in Stratego, so operational wargames could field opponents that feint and conceal force composition at calibrated rates.
Bargaining with hidden reservation values is an imperfect-information game; equilibrium strategies bluff and concede in ways scripted thresholds cannot.
Competitors with private costs or plans can bluff in price wars and market entry, and designers can measure how exploitable a fixed AI pricing script is by computing a best response against it.

Equilibrium strategies put a value on information, so AI opponents scout, hide their own attributes, and avoid revealing them through their actions, giving the player's scouting system a real counterpart.

Difficulty-conditioned generators let the next map or wave be built at a target difficulty instead of multiplying enemy counts, though EA SEED's match-3 model hit the requested difficulty only a third of the time.
Text-to-level models small enough to run on the client (MarioGPT has 96M parameters) let players request maps in words at runtime, extending generated content from text and items to playable space.

Hand-written noise and placement rules give way to a generator trained on example maps or prompted with text, so a seed becomes a prompt plus a sample, and validity must be checked by a solver instead of guaranteed by construction.
Scenario maps can be produced from a written description of the situation, Word2World-style story to world, with an agent playthrough confirming the stated goal is reachable.
Motion-matching-quality responsive locomotion fits in a few MB of weights, making it affordable on memory-constrained platforms and for more character types.
Players author new character motions from their own video (inZOI), so the animation set available to life-sim characters is no longer fixed by the studio's mocap library.
Voters become LLM agents that hear persuasion from other agents and vote on amendments, as in Project Sid's constitutional votes, instead of computing a vote from satisfaction and bloc membership.
Memes, beliefs, and a seeded religion spread through populations of 500 to one million agents, with content mutating in conversation and spread shaped by social structure or a recommender feed.

Roles emerge from agents' social context and goals (farmers, miners, guards in 30-agent villages) rather than from job slots filled by education level; AgentSociety adds agent-level employment and consumption decisions.
Unplayed households can be advanced by cheap language-agent societies that generate plausible life events instead of fixed event tables.

A shared world can be populated by hundreds of autonomous agents that keep roles, culture, and rules while human players come and go; PIANO was built for real-time interaction with humans and other agents.
NPC populations can propose, debate, and vote on rule changes in natural language and then comply or not, so legislation is no longer limited to human players in a shared world.

A policy's effect on groups is measured by running it on a population of agents (AgentSociety's universal basic income and hurricane experiments) instead of reading hand-authored weighted edges from policies to voter groups.
Tax compliance becomes an agent decision that responds to law changes and influencer messaging, as in Project Sid's 20% tax experiment, rather than an automatic deduction at the set rate.
Advisors can answer arbitrary player questions about the current situation and recommend actions in context, instead of speaking a fixed catalog of threshold-triggered messages.
The inspection panel can answer why an agent did something by summarizing its needs, itemized mood terms, and recent thought log into a short causal account.
A long nested modifier chain can be condensed into a ranked plain-language list of the largest causes and what would change them, while the numbers still come from the simulation.
Recorded events can be retold as biographies, recaps, or highlight summaries for the player, a commentator and reteller role.
Graph changes can be annotated with narrated causes drawn from the event log, such as which policy or disaster preceded a drop.
Story continuation from Do, Say, Story, and See inputs makes the whole narrative generated content; grounded engines turn it into typed state changes.

Any typed action is adjudicated for plausibility and consequence rather than matched against a parser's verb list, so unanticipated approaches produce new narrative paths (53 emergent nodes in one 28-player study).
NPCs with backstories, goals, and personality are generated from designer criteria and voiced in dialogue, removing per-character writing.

The director can author an event in language for the exact current state, check it against canon and rules, and narrate it, instead of choosing among a finite catalog of pre-written incidents by a pacing budget.
Follow-up beats are generated from story state and player intent rather than scheduled by authored templates with trigger predicates, while the player still experiences multi-step chains.

Characters can ask for things tied to the specific story so far, not only fetch templates with filled slots; ungrounded models invent quests that do not exist, so requests must be checked against state.
Collections become open-ended races to discover never-generated items, with a First Discovery credit for the first player to create each one.
A language model decides the result of each new combination and caches it, turning a finite authored recipe graph into an open one (Infinite Craft).
Generated results are written back as shared, persistent rules rather than one-off text, so the world's content grows with play and stays consistent across players.
The recipe space becomes unbounded: any pair of items yields a generated result rather than a lookup in a finite designer table, and the first answer is cached as the permanent recipe.

Interactions between arbitrary materials or elements can be resolved by a model rather than an authored pair table, but whole-state accuracy near 60% means results must be bounded to simple outputs and cached.
Millions of simulated matches per hour let designers check how attribute weights and tactic modifiers shift outcome distributions before shipping a match-engine change.
Locomotion policies train in seconds to minutes on one GPU (Brax, MuJoCo Playground), so a creature could learn to move or act through RL during a play session instead of from canned animation.
A player design can be scored over hundreds of randomized loads, terrains or seeds in parallel, giving a robustness distribution instead of one deterministic test run.

A player-built creature or machine can be dropped into thousands of parallel worlds and have a controller trained for its specific body, so assembled designs move competently without the player programming them.
Fitness can be measured by simulating every individual of a large population in its own physics world each generation, so selection acts on actual behavior rather than on summed stat values.
Batched GPU rigid-body solvers step thousands of worlds or bodies per kernel launch, so physics-heavy evaluation that was CPU-bound becomes cheap enough for large sweeps.
GPUDrive shows multi-agent vehicle simulation above one million steps per second, which points to agent-level traffic at counts where city builders now fall back to aggregate flow.
Cheap batched rollouts make it practical to search utility-curve weights, or train a policy to replace them, against metrics such as survival or need satisfaction over many simulated colonies.
One equilibrium policy over positions serves any number of agents, like a flow field that already includes congestion effects, replacing per-agent searches.
Park visitors can choose attractions in equilibrium with expected queues and crowding rather than greedily, producing realistic spreading of crowds across a park.
Queue choice and arrival timing become equilibrium behavior, so changing capacity at one service shifts load across the others as people anticipate the change.
Prices can come from many small rational producers and consumers in equilibrium (as in MFG models of energy markets), instead of a fixed elasticity formula.

Trip routing changes from each agent reacting to current travel times, which oscillates, to an equilibrium in which drivers anticipate congestion, computed once for the population at a cost independent of car count.
Mode split solved as a population equilibrium in which each traveler responds to congestion created by everyone else.
Ensembles (50 GenCast members) give calibrated probabilities, so an in-game forecast can carry real uncertainty that players plan against and that occasionally misses honestly.
Earth-system foundation models fine-tuned to several domains suggest climate sims coupling atmosphere, ocean waves and air chemistry, though they are trained for days-ahead weather, not decades.
Aurora's fine-tuned air-quality forecasts run about 100,000x faster than CAMS, a path to pollution plumes transported by simulated wind at playable cost.
Storms emerge from atmospheric state with forecastable tracks (Aurora beat operational centres on 5-day cyclone tracks), turning disasters from dice rolls into threats with lead time.
Weather becomes a coherent global field with fronts, cyclones and multi-day evolution across hundreds of variables, instead of a per-region Markov chain of weather states.

Sample-efficient model-based learners (EfficientZero needed about two hours of experience) make it plausible for a creature to learn new behaviors from player reward within a session, by planning in a learned model of its world rather than reacting with a fixed network.

Opponents plan with a learned value function plus search over unit actions, giving strong play in operational simulations where hand-written doctrine is brittle; latent models allow planning where exact rollouts are too slow.
Each toggle combination is a rule variant; converged self-play under each variant measures how much a policy shifts outcomes and flags toggles that are strictly dominant or never worth enacting.

Competitor AI becomes a policy trained by self-play against the game's own rules, so it re-adapts when economic rules change in a patch instead of needing rewritten heuristics; training compute per rule set is the cost.
Self-play agents trained on each candidate tree reveal dominant research orders and unused branches, the same comparison AlphaZero made across chess rule variants.
Governors or managers given a subsystem can search over action sequences toward the player-set goal with the same forward model, staying competent in rule configurations designers did not script for.

AI factions can weigh war, peace, and alliance options by simulating future turns of the campaign, the kind of high-level campaign decision Total War: Rome II gave to MCTS, so choices respond to the actual strategic position instead of fixed opinion thresholds.

Tactical AI plans multi-unit action sequences within a time budget, as in Fable Legends' real-time tactical planning, rather than following scripted doctrine; the iteration budget becomes a difficulty lever.

AI competitors can pick prices, expansions, and acquisitions by rolling the economic model forward, so rival play adapts to the player's position and to rule changes without bespoke heuristics per market rule.

Agents choose actions by sampling futures from the game's forward model and backing up outcomes, instead of scoring one-step options with hand-tuned utility curves, so choices account for consequences several actions ahead at a per-decision compute cost.
In WHAMM the avatar's movement and camera are rendered by the model from controller input, at 10+ fps with a 0.9 second context.
Designers insert an object or character into a frame and the model generates plausible gameplay around it (persistency), giving a preview of how a content change might play before it is built.

Movement and collisions follow learned game dynamics; the Nature paper's consistency criterion is that generated play respects controller input and the game's physics, which is measured statistically rather than enforced.

Local per-cell material rules can be learned from examples of desired behavior instead of hand-coded; DiffLogic CA recovered Game of Life exactly as a compact logic circuit cheap enough for per-pixel use.
A seed block placed by the player can grow into a castle or tree over time under a learned 3D rule, a growth-based alternative to instant procedural detailing.
Tile maps and levels can be grown by NCA generators selected by quality-diversity search for solvability and diversity, replacing hand-tuned noise and placement rules.
Regenerating NCA regrow damaged shapes and 3D NCA regrow parts of machines, enabling destructible structures and organisms that heal from local rules rather than respawning.

Neural denoising and the neural radiance cache make dynamic multi-bounce lighting affordable, so player-built interiors and towns can be lit correctly across a full diurnal cycle where baked lighting cannot follow player construction.

Up to 7x VRAM savings from neural texture compression and cheaper layered materials let more distinct high-detail decor assets be resident at once, raising the variety a beauty-driven builder can show on screen.

Upscaling and frame generation raise displayed frame rates in GPU-heavy flight and driving sims for the same render cost; generated frames do not sample new input, so frame generation adds latency that hurts precise hand-flying or driving.
Total War: PHARAOH's ACE advisor answers questions about the game's systems from a small on-device model connected to game data, instead of firing authored lines when indicators cross thresholds.
Characters generate text thoughts about events and reflect on past decisions, giving each agent a running inner monologue rather than a list of authored mood modifiers.
Free-text and voice input to characters runs on the player's GPU, removing per-token server cost and network round trips, so open conversation can be offered to every player of a premium game.
A co-playable teammate such as PUBG Ally takes spoken orders about movement, looting, and strategy mid-match and acts on them, a command channel that needs no menus or ping wheel.
Smart Zois pick actions with a small model that reads needs, surroundings, and inner thoughts rather than only scored need curves, while the game's action set stays the same.
Challenge scales with measured learning progress per task family rather than with wealth or time survived, using a band that admits only tasks the current agent or player can partly solve.
A creature or companion can improve through self-proposed practice tasks with model-estimated rewards, the loop SIMA 2 used, rather than only through explicit player reward and punishment.

Terrain parameters are mutated against measured agent or player performance, as POET did with walker terrain roughness, gaps, and stumps, so maps grow harder along the axes a player has already mastered.

Objectives stop being a fixed authored list: a model writes each task and its success check as code, admitted only if it is neither already solved nor out of reach, so a sandbox can keep issuing new challenges.
Requests can be generated beyond fixed templates, with completion conditions written as generated code over simulation state and an archive of past requests used to avoid repeats.
Mirage 2 lets players save and share generated worlds; what is shared is a prompt and seed image for a model rather than an asset bundle, so the receiver needs the same hosted model.
Walking, turning, and jumping are rendered from a unified camera-action space; GameCraft's action space lacks shooting, throwing, and explosions.
Typed text during play adds or restyles objects and scenes (Yan editing, Mirage 2 commands, Odyssey-2 prompts), so content is requested at runtime rather than authored.

A world starts from any image, sketch, or photo (Mirage 2, GameCraft); pose-indexed memory in Matrix-Game 3.0 and WorldPlay lets revisited areas stay consistent for about a minute, still far short of a save file.
Contact and motion responses come from video priors; out-of-domain views degrade (Matrix-Game 2.0 reports over-saturation under sustained upward or forward camera motion).
Matrix-Game 2.0 was fine-tuned on 574 hours of GTA driving; car handling is reproduced from video rather than tire and suspension models, with no guarantee of consistent grip or mass.
Learned video dynamics could stand in for a physics engine in open-ended scenes, but near-chance IntPhys 2 scores show current models do not reliably reject impossible motion.
V-JEPA 2-AC scores candidate action sequences by predicted distance to a goal image in latent space, a learned alternative to hand-written utility curves for agents whose goals can be pictured.

Cosmos is positioned for autonomous-vehicle training and closed-loop evaluation; a driving model post-trained from it predicts scene video under driving inputs with no tire or suspension model, which suits traffic scenarios more than the handling fidelity a racing sim needs.
The controlled character becomes a physical body that adapts footing to terrain and reacts to pushes, instead of playing canned clips that slide over geometry.

With a simulated body, a wound could change gait by limiting joint torque instead of swapping in an authored limp; the cited work does not demonstrate injury-conditioned motion, so this remains a projection.
Characters join the rigid-body simulation as actuated bodies, so carried, pushed, and collided objects affect them and vice versa (InterMimic human-object interaction).

When an object advertises an interaction (sit, lie, lean), a goal-conditioned controller can perform it on new furniture geometry without a bespoke animation per object, as MaskedMimic shows for chairs, stools, and sofas.
Searching for the top-scoring design in every descriptor cell stress-tests the rating formula and surfaces degenerate designs that score well, such as rides or bridges that game the metric.
Searches over module and beacon layouts expose dominant boosting configurations that collapse design choice.

Mapping the build space by behavior descriptors, as was done for Hearthstone decks, shows the best design in each style niche, exposing dominant part combinations and empty niches before players find them.

Instead of one seed-to-map generator, a game can ship an archive of maps spanning designer axes, such as resource density by chokepoint count, each verified by simulation and served to players by trait.
An archive of competitor strategies, each the strongest found for its niche (aggressive expander, low-price discounter), gives AI rivals distinct styles without hand-tuning each persona.
Scenario maps and starting conditions can be generated across a difficulty-by-style grid and filtered by agent playthroughs, replacing hand-built scenario sets with a curated archive.
Players or in-world logic change the whole world's look at runtime by text, without new textures or models; the game's systems cannot read the new look, so it carries no gameplay meaning.
Blocky player builds are rendered as detailed structures in a prompted style (for example Roman), a visual-only form of build assist: collision and block state stay coarse while the view is detailed.

Characters can hold spoken, interruptible, full-duplex conversations with response onset near human turn-taking, replacing dialogue wheels or typed input; Whispers from the Star is built around this loop.
Generated characters can get distinct designed or cloned voices and speak unscripted lines without recording sessions, which removes the voice-acting cost that keeps procedural characters silent.
Delivery carries social meaning (whispering, sighing, hesitation, warmth) generated from conversational context, so the same line can land as a flirt, apology, or threat.
Squad orders can be spoken mid-action and parsed into function calls, as in PUBG Ally's voice-directed teammate, without menus.

Recognizable real buildings and landmarks across the planet make visual navigation by reference to the ground practicable anywhere, extending hand-flying practice beyond hand-modeled airports and cities.

The world is reconstructed from real imagery instead of generated from a seed and noise; the player-facing role of an explorable map is unchanged, but its content is the real planet, with procedural filling only where imagery is missing.
Learned classification of satellite imagery turns real-world map data into simulated scenery at planetary scale (Microsoft Flight Simulator).
Treating target survival-time or loss-rate distributions from playtest telemetry as the observation, the posterior gives scaling parameters that reproduce them and how sensitive each one is.
Match-engine parameters can be fitted so simulated score and statistic distributions match real league data, with uncertainty on each parameter.
Transmission, recovery and contact parameters can be inferred from real outbreak curves or target curves, with a posterior that shows which parameters the data cannot pin down.
Predator-prey rates can be inferred from target population time series, so designers state desired oscillations and the posterior returns rates that produce them.
Economic ABM parameters can be calibrated to price and quantity time series (Dyer et al.), grounding market sims in real data instead of hand-set elasticities.
Demand and route-choice parameters of an agent-based traffic model can be fitted to observed counts, the same likelihood-free ABM calibration applied to a city.
Hands-on tasks such as surgery or handling soft objects could show tissue and cloth reacting plausibly to tools in real time, adding feedback the player reads to perform the skill.
Deformation learned from an offline solver runs 300-5000x faster than that solver, putting near-offline-quality cloth and flesh response within a real-time budget.
Decor and furniture catalogs that beauty and environment scores consume can be produced from prompts or reference images in seconds per asset, so catalog size stops being bounded by modeling time.
Runtime generation extends from text and textures to placeable 3D props: inZOI players convert their own images into in-game objects.

Part-controllable generation (Roblox CubePart) produces assets split into parts intended for physics and scripts, which could supply new components for build-from-parts mechanics on request; not yet shown in a shipped assembly game.
An NPC's competence can be an accumulating library of composable, verified routines it wrote itself, so skill growth adds new behaviors rather than raising a numeric speed or quality level.
A delegated controller can acquire routines for situations its designers did not code by writing and verifying new functions, instead of running the fixed opponent-AI logic restricted to a subsystem.

Turns run from 4000 BC to as late as AD 2100; each turn every city produces and every unit moves, against two to seven AI civilizations.
Scenarios are shared through the Steam Workshop.
Units are assigned to patrol, strike, and support missions and executed by tactical AI under doctrine settings such as weapon release authority and EMCON.
Each side sees only what its sensors detect; emission control (EMCON) policies trade a unit's own detection range against revealing it to enemy passive sensors.

Every platform's sensors and weapons come from a database of tens of thousands of real systems; radar propagation, sensor degradation, terrain masking, sonar thermal layers, weather, jamming, and anti-radiation strikes are modeled for thousands of active platforms in real time.
A Lua scripting engine and scenario editor let players build custom operations.
Ballistics are among the modeled effects alongside sensor propagation, so weapon flight and impact follow database specifications.
Over 600 official and community scenarios plus a quick battle generator.
Contacts begin unidentified and are classified as sensor data accumulates.
Direct orders override a unit's mission behavior.
Scenarios lasting hours to days of game time run with time acceleration and pause.
Weather degrades sensors and affects engagements.
Cash from inspections, foiled smuggling, and interventions pays for upgrades while post maintenance costs rise over time.
The player walks the post in first person, opens and searches vehicles, drives upgradable police cars in pursuits, and uses firearms in shootouts.
Gang attacks on the post are countered with purchased defense upgrades.
Drivers present documents whose number grows over the campaign; small discrepancies require refusal, and suspicious vehicles are searched with a UV flashlight before tools extract hidden goods.
Special assignments and story decisions shape the fate of Acaristan and lead to multiple endings.
Grendels steal food, injure Norns, and carry diseases that sicken the population.
Exported Norns and genomes were swapped and bred across players by a large online community.
The player's hand pointer feeds Norns, shows them objects, and tickles or slaps them; neglect leads to hunger, disease, and death, but care shapes behavior only indirectly through learning.

A neural-network brain maps sensed objects and drives to actions; drive reduction reinforces the action that preceded it, and the hand's tickle and slap act as reward and punishment through the same pathway.
Norns hatch, grow, breed, and die within roughly 40 hours of play.
Players teach nouns by naming objects a Norn is looking at and verbs with a learning computer, then type instructions that the Norn may choose to obey.
Drives such as hunger and tiredness are concentrations in a simulated biochemistry that rise over time and fall when actions such as eating or resting succeed.
Haploid digital genomes with no dominant or recessive genes encode brain wiring, biochemistry, and organs; offspring genomes mutate, and every boxed copy shipped a unique starting set of egg genomes.
Skills grow from education and from perks in six lifestyles, each with three skill trees.
Nested tooltips let players open explanations of terms inside other tooltips.
Counties carry a faith and a culture; the court chaplain can convert a county's faith and the steward can promote the ruler's culture, while faith hostility sets opinion penalties from 0 to -30.

On death, play passes to the player heir and titles pass under the realm's succession law, so partition can split a realm among children; the game ends if no viable heir remains, and dynasty heads spend Renown on bonuses for every dynasty member.
Wars are fought over claims, and marriages and alliances link realms.

Each character's opinion of another is an itemized list of modifiers from traits, relations, actions, and events, many expiring over time; discontented vassals join factions pressing for independence, a rival claimant, or less crown authority.
Personality, education, and genetic traits modify the six skills (Diplomacy, Martial, Stewardship, Intrigue, Learning, Prowess), opinions, and which event options a character can take.
Prestige and piety accrue from rank, traits, and deeds and are spent on actions such as creating titles (prestige) and faith decisions (piety).
Friends, rivals, and lovers form between characters and shift opinions and event outcomes.
Marriages create alliances and heirs, making match choice a political decision.
Vassal factions accumulate strength and can revolt when their demands are refused.
Battles resolve from army size, men-at-arms, knights, commander skill, and terrain, in phases that run until one side is routed.

Acting against personality traits and suffering events add stress; crossing stress levels fires mental-break events whose coping options can add traits (from level 2 up), and extreme stress can kill the character.
Lifestyle perk trees and cultural innovations unlock abilities and buildings.
Counties belong to titles with de jure hierarchies, and wars are fought to press claims on them; conquered counties start with low county control.
Genetic traits such as strong or poor health pass to children.
Events are called from on_actions, decisions, and interactions, with weighted options and scheduled follow-ups.
War score from battles and occupation lets the attacker enforce the war goal at full score, while either side can offer white peace.
Aircraft modules are built from real-world data; the F-16C uses a professional flight model with a fly-by-wire flight control system.
Missions pit aircraft against air and ground units with sensors and weapons; users host PvE and PvP servers running their own missions.
Lua mission scripting and third-party module development extend the platform.
Clickable cockpits operate modeled engines, fuel, electrical, hydraulic, and radio systems, so start-up and weapon employment follow real procedures.
Missiles, bombs, and gun rounds fly as simulated projectiles, so release parameters such as speed, altitude, and range decide hits.
The mission editor builds single-player and multiplayer missions with Lua scripting.
Modules carry damage models, revised over the platform's development, so hits degrade the aircraft's modeled systems and how it flies.
Dilemmas, such as appointing a senior judge, must be resolved before the turn can end.
Before each general election the player makes two promises to the electorate; broken promises raise voter cynicism, and losing the election ends the game.

Voter groups such as the religious, patriotic, parents, capitalists, socialists, liberals, and conservatives overlap, since each voter belongs to several, so pleasing every group is nearly impossible.
Deficits add to national debt that the player must pay down.

Policies in seven areas (tax, economy, welfare, foreign policy, transport, law and order, public services) are sliders; the engine treats voters, groups, policies, ministers, and events as neurons in a homebrew network with bounded values, so weighted effects move statistics such as crime and air quality and the happiness of voter groups.
Introducing or cancelling a policy costs political capital.
Political capital, earned through loyal ministers, is spent each turn to introduce, cancel, or adjust policies, so it caps how fast the government can change.
Excessive taxes cause tax evasion.
Situations such as pollution or homelessness persist while conditions hold, and events arrive outside player control.
Hound attacks scale with days survived, from 2 hounds every 5-8 days early to 7-10 hounds every 11-16 days after day 100, with shorter warnings.

A day lasts 8 real minutes in sixteen 30-second segments of day, dusk, and night; sanity drains 5 per minute at dusk and 50 per minute in total darkness, where Charlie attacks unless the player has light.
Fire spreads across flammable plants and structures.
Recipes combine gathered items into tools, light, shelter, and weapons; most must first be prototyped at a crafting station such as the science machine, though some characters bypass this.
Death deletes the world unless a rare resurrection item is available.
Each world is randomly generated.
Picked grass, saplings, and berry bushes regrow.
Winter shortens days and lengthens nights; seasons change hazards.
Food spoils over time; spoiled food restores less hunger and costs health and sanity.
Hunger, health, and sanity meters; default maximum hunger is 150 and drains 75 per game day, and at empty hunger health drains 1.25 per second until the player eats or dies.
Wealthier and more populous fortresses attract sieges and megabeasts.
Work quality and speed rise with skill gained through practice in each labor.
A justice system punishes assault, murder, and vandalism.
Underground farming on soil layers; plump helmet mushrooms are brewed into wine.
The player designates digging, chopping, construction, and workshop jobs; dwarves with the matching labor enabled pick them up, and a manager can queue work orders automatically.
Fires spread and burn dwarves and furniture.
Water and magma flow tile by tile with up to seven depth levels per tile, so breaching a river, cavern lake, or magma source floods connected tunnels.
Dwarves carry goods to player-defined stockpiles.
Tiles, materials, and creatures carry temperatures.
Legends mode lists historical figures, sites, artifacts, and civilizations with a historical map; fortress deeds and retired adventurers are added, and the archive exports to XML.

World generation builds elevation, rainfall, drainage, temperature, and vegetation layers, then simulates civilizations, sites, and historical figures for a player-chosen number of years before the fortress is embarked.
Migrant waves from the mountainhome grow as the fortress develops.

Body parts are layered tissues (skin, fat, muscle, bone, nerves) damaged individually in combat; injuries can be permanent and are treated in a hospital with traction benches, casts, sutures, and splints.
Emotions become short-term memories; strong or revisited ones are promoted to long-term memories that keep adding stress.

Emotions add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000; stressed dwarves throw tantrums, fall into depression, or wander obliviously, prolonged stress leads to insanity, and one breakdown can spread unhappiness.
Food, drink, and sleep, plus personal needs such as socializing or praying met at taverns, temples, and libraries.
Facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale how stress builds and dissipates.
Ore is smelted to bars and alloyed; steel needs flux to make pig iron plus coke or charcoal, and magma can replace fuel.
Ambushes, sieges, megabeasts, and forgotten beasts are met with squads, fortifications, and traps triggered by levers or pressure plates.
Friends, family, and pets; their deaths are major stressors.
Furniture defines bedrooms, dining halls, and offices; nobles demand rooms of rising value.

Emotions from events add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) scaled by facets such as stress vulnerability and bravery; above +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000 dwarves risk tantrums, depression, obliviousness, and insanity, and long-term memories keep adding stress.
Yearly caravans from neighboring civilizations are handled by a broker; caravans can be absent or hostile depending on history.
Military squads in uniforms train at barracks and can be ordered to attack.
Z-levels, added in 2007, let the fortress descend level by level through soil and stone to caverns, the magma sea, and the underworld, connected by stairs and ramps.
Dark Fog threat accumulates from the player's power generation and from combat, bases and hives gain levels from experience, and aggressiveness settings scale attack sizes.
Layouts are saved and pasted as blueprints, and the mech's construction drones place them.
Three belt tiers carry items between sorters and machines on a planetary grid that wraps around a sphere and narrows toward the poles.
Planets rotate around their axes and orbit their stars, so solar panel output varies with the local day.
The player flies the Icarus mech across planets and through space to build within its range.
The Icarus mech hand-crafts early buildings from inventory before assemblers take over.
Proliferator coating on input items lets the consuming machine choose extra products or faster production.

The Dyson sphere is designed in a node-and-frame editor and built from solar sails fired by EM-Rail Ejectors and frames carried by rockets; unabsorbed sails expire after 5,400 seconds, and the finished sphere's energy feeds endgame production.
The Dyson sphere editor places nodes, frames, and shells on multiple orbital layers around a star, and its power output depends on built structure and absorbed sails.

Wind, thermal, solar, fusion, and artificial-star generators feed tower-linked grids; logistics stations charge at 30 to 300 MW, and Dyson sphere energy reaches planets through ray receivers at 30% base efficiency.
Each seed generates a star cluster with star types, planet types, and mineral distributions, including neutron stars, white dwarfs, and black holes.

Smelters, assemblers, chemical plants, refineries, and particle colliders run fixed recipes that build up to six matrix cube types and Dyson sphere components; proliferator coating adds extra products or speed.
Dark Fog planetary bases and space hives attack factories and the player's mech, countered by turrets, energy shields, and player combat units.

Logistics stations set each item slot to local or remote supply, demand, or storage and are paired automatically by priority; up to 100 drones per station haul within a planet and 10 vessels between planets, with range and minimum-load sliders.
Mining machines and advanced miners extract iron, copper, titanium, silicon, and rare veins whose distribution differs by planet and star type; pumps and oil extractors tap fluids.
Storage boxes, tanks, and per-slot capacity in logistics stations buffer flows between planets.
Labs in research mode consume matrix cubes in technology-specific mixes, all stacked labs working on the front of one queue; labs can instead be switched to manufacture matrices.
Varied food and larger homes earn skill points spent on specialties such as farming, hunting, trade, and engineering.
Players post labor contracts for others to fulfill.
A meteor is set to strike in thirty days, and players must gather resources and research technology to stop it without harming the world.
Thousands of plants and animals from dozens of species grow across the world; overhunting or overharvesting can drive a species extinct, and a disruption in one species cascades across the planet.
Accumulated pollution changes the climate and sea level.
Players run stores and currency exchanges with fiat or resource-backed currencies and set exchange rates.

Players propose laws in a programmable rule system and vote on them, the game enforces ratified laws, and elections set tax rates and community funds; governments range from dictatorships to lawless, trust-based communities.
Mining waste and industrial pollution poison rivers and kill farms, and excessive air pollution raises sea levels.
More than 30 craft tables turn materials into goods across hundreds of recipes.
Plant and animal populations recover over time unless harvested faster than they regrow; cutting too many trees reduces how much air pollution is absorbed.
Each world is bounded by a meteor due in thirty days, so a server's run ends with stopping it or with impact, and servers are commonly wiped and restarted as fresh worlds.
Real-time wireframe dogfights and manual docking that requires matching a rotating station's spin unless a docking computer is bought.
Combat rating rises with kills from Harmless toward Elite; most versions also offer Galactic Navy missions with special rewards.
Eight galaxies of 256 planets each are generated from seed numbers at runtime; each system's name, economy, government, and description derive from the seed.
Legal status (clean, offender, fugitive) worsens with piracy and illegal cargo and draws police ships.
Mining lasers break asteroids into fragments that can be scooped and sold.
Commodity prices vary by system economy; the player buys cheap and sells dear between systems, constrained by cargo bay size and the 7 light-year fuel limit per jump.
Mission boards offer delivery, combat, and data missions with deadlines and payouts that also move faction influence.
Six-axis Newtonian flight with optional flight assist; manual docking, supercruise approaches, and combat that balances power distributor pips and heat.
Minor factions hold influence shares per system and enter wars or elections when two factions' influence is close; Powerplay pledges players to one of 12 powers contesting territory.
System bodies are unknown until scanned; first discoverers are credited.
Ship heat rises from weapons, fuel scooping near stars, and damage; overheating damages modules, and heat sinks dump it.
Ships take modules in fixed slots (power plant, thrusters, frame shift drive, hardpoints); module mass and class set jump range, speed, and loadout.
One galaxy state is shared by Open, Private Group, and Solo players; Frontier's Background Simulation changes faction influence, system states, and markets over time from aggregate player activity.
Squadrons and player-supported minor factions coordinate background simulation work.

The power distributor's pips are split among systems, engines, and weapons capacitors in flight, setting each capacitor's recharge; module priorities decide what shuts down when the power plant is over budget.
A power plant's output must cover module draw; over budget, modules shut down by player-set priority.
Stellar Forge generates a 1:1 Milky Way of about 400 billion systems, bodies, and landable planetary surfaces, blended with about 150,000 catalog systems.
About 150,000 star systems from real astronomical catalogs are blended into the procedurally generated galaxy.
Standing with minor factions and superpower navy ranks gate missions and system permits.
Mining lasers, collector limpets, and sub-surface charges extract ore from planetary rings.
Each ship module has its own integrity, and damage to the power plant, thrusters, or drive degrades or disables it until repaired.
Market supply and demand at each station shift prices as players buy and sell.
Station markets differ by economy type; traders haul commodities between stations for price differences, limited by cargo capacity and jump range.
Diversity points earned by healthy plants and animals are the single currency for buying species, modifications, and evolutions; repeatable tasks let players farm a steady income.
Some animals hunt others, so predator placement constrains prey populations.
Each species needs a biome, food, and nearby plants or water; satisfied individuals stay healthy, live longer, and breed, while unmet needs reduce health.
Plants and animals grow, eat, reproduce, and die on species-specific cycles.
Species evolve into new species once their conditions are met and points are paid, and 60+ tasks grant points or content.
Planted grasses convert ground into one of 10 biome types, and algae turns water into river for fish.
Skill points from experience unlock ADR, long-distance, valuable, fragile, urgent, and eco-driving jobs.
Jobs specify cargo, destination, and a time limit; less damage earns more money and experience, while fuel, tolls, and repairs are paid from earnings.
A bank loan is the alternative to saving 100,000 euros for the first truck.
A continuous road map linking European cities sets route distance, tolls, and travel time.
Recruitment agencies supply AI drivers who work from owned garages and return income.
Licensed trucks with modeled engines and gearboxes pull trailers whose cargo changes acceleration and braking; collisions damage truck, trailer, and cargo.
Damage requires paid maintenance at service shops.

A national corruption value accumulates from several state conditions and falls with a monthly budget line for rooting out corruption; while high it raises the cost of technology and other state actions.
Provinces have a culture and a religion; missionaries convert province religion over time against resistance, and non-state religion or non-accepted culture adds unrest.
Each monarch's administrative, diplomatic, and military skill sets monthly monarch point income; on death an heir succeeds, with risks of regency, succession wars, or personal unions.
Alliances, vassals, tributaries, and royal marriages bind nations; aggressive expansion raises other nations' hostility until they form a defensive coalition against the expander.
Estates hold loyalty and influence over the crown and grant bonuses or demands.
Deficits are covered by loans, and unmanageable debt ends in bankruptcy.
AI opinion of the player is an itemized sum of modifiers such as improved relations, royal marriage, and aggressive expansion.
Idea groups, policies, and government reforms change national rules.

Administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch points accrue monthly from the ruler's skills (plus advisors) and buy technology, ideas, stability, and province development, so each succession changes the nation's budget of action.
Prestige and power projection modify diplomacy and stability.
Provinces accumulate unrest from foreign culture, religion, and recent conquest, and high unrest spawns rebel armies; national stability is a separate stock raised with administrative monarch points.
Land battles roll dice each phase of fire and shock, modified by general skill and terrain, and drain each army's strength and morale until one side retreats.
Administrative, diplomatic, and military technology tracks are bought with matching monarch points; institutions such as feudalism spread between provinces and raise technology cost until embraced.

Provinces have an owner and a controller; sieges flip control, peace deals transfer ownership, and new provinces must be cored with administrative power, with uncored land adding overextension and unrest.

Trade value generated in provinces flows downstream through a fixed directed network of trade nodes; merchants either collect in a node or steer value toward the player's home node, and trade power in each node sets the share taken.
Historical and flavor events fire from national history and current state.
War score from battles, occupation, and the war goal caps peace demands, each priced in score (provinces, gold, vassalage).
Skills have prerequisites, and capital-ship skills take several times longer to train than frigate skills.
Players elect the Council of Stellar Management, which carries requests to CCP; the first election in 2008 had 66 candidates for nine seats.
A destroyed ship and its fittings are gone for good, part of its cargo and modules drops in a lootable wreck, and ship insurance pays back part of the hull's value.
Ships are fitted with modules in high, mid, and low slots plus semi-permanent rigs.

One shared universe on the Tranquility server holds more than 5,000 stargate-linked systems plus about 2,500 wormhole systems; system security from 1.0 to -1.0 sets whether CONCORD police destroy aggressors.

Players gather raw materials and manufacture nearly all ships and modules, then trade them in a supply-and-demand market with price history charts, where manipulation such as ramping and bear raids is possible.
Corporations led by a CEO assign roles, tax members, declare wars for a weekly fee, and join alliances that claim sovereignty over null-sec systems.
Blueprints turn gathered materials into ships and modules.

Each system's security from 1.0 to -1.0 decides whether CONCORD police destroy aggressors; high-sec deters player attacks, low- and null-sec leave them to players, and the riskier zones hold the richer activities.
Skills train in real time, including while logged off, from a queue of up to 50 skills.
Unprovoked aggression in secure space costs security status and draws police response.
Players mine asteroids and salvage wrecks for materials.
The player walks around the apartment in first person and can click objects or body parts to hug, comfort, or kiss.
Typed sentences are matched by keywords and context to discourse acts such as agreeing, criticizing, or flirting, which Grace and Trip answer in character.
As the couple argues, the player's responses read as taking one side, which shapes later beats.
A drama manager chooses the next beat whose preconditions match the state, steering toward a rising tension arc and one of three endings.
Revelations such as a confessed affair fire only when earlier beats and player choices set them up.
An evolution factor rises with elapsed time, total pollution produced, and spawners destroyed, squashed as total over one plus total, and unlocks medium, big, and behemoth enemies.
Selected areas save to blueprints, books, and a personal library that persists across saves; exchange strings are shared online, and construction robots build pasted ghosts.
Two-lane belts in four tiers carry 15, 30, 45, or 60 items per second; splitters, undergrounds, and lane priorities shape flow, and inserters move items between belts and machines.
Ore tiles run out as they are mined, and crude oil wells decline toward a 20% yield floor, pushing expansion to new patches.
The engineer walks the map, mines by hand early, and places buildings within reach, later driving cars, tanks, and spidertrons.
Pipes and pumps carry water, crude oil, petroleum, and steam; version 2.0 merged pipes into segments that share contents.
The engineer crafts early buildings and items from inventory using the same recipes as assemblers, with a crafting queue.

Speed, productivity, efficiency, and (Space Age) quality modules fill machine slots, and beacons project module effects onto neighboring machines at a power cost; productivity bonuses are capped at +300%.
The rocket silo consumes rocket parts for each launch, and launching a rocket ends the base game; Space Age moves the goal to a space platform reaching the edge of the solar system.
Mods use a modified Lua 5.2 with data and control stages and are distributed through an in-game mod portal; overhauls such as Krastorio 2 replace progression.
Machines emit pollution into 32x32 chunks; above 15 units a chunk diffuses 2% to each cardinal neighbor every 64 ticks, and water, grass, and trees absorb it.
Steam engines, solar panels, accumulators, and nuclear reactors feed a pole-connected grid; under shortage power is shared evenly so all machines slow proportionally.
Maps are generated from a seed with settings for ore frequency, size, and richness, water, cliffs, and enemy bases.
Assembling machines, furnaces, chemical plants, and refineries run fixed recipes with crafting times; science packs require multi-step trees from ore to circuits, oil products, and rocket parts.
The Space Age expansion adds five quality levels from normal to legendary, raised by chance from quality modules, with a recycler that returns 25% of ingredients.

Biter and spitter nests send attack groups when their chunk absorbs pollution, recruiting units at pollution costs from 4 for a small biter to 400 for a behemoth; turrets, walls, and flamethrowers defend.
Rail and chain signals divide track into blocks that one train reserves at a time, letting train networks share track.

Roboports define logistic zones where logistic robots carry items among active provider, passive provider, storage, buffer, and requester chests by priority, one item per trip at 3 tiles per second before research.
Electric and burner mining drills extract iron, copper, coal, stone, and uranium from ore patches at rates set by drill tier and mining productivity research; pumpjacks extract crude oil.
Red and green wires carry item-count signals into arithmetic, decider, constant, and (in 2.0) selector combinators that control inserters, belts, train stops, and lamps.
In Space Age, Gleba's agricultural products spoil over fixed timers into spoilage, and recipe outputs inherit ingredient freshness.
Production and consumption graphs per item over time windows and an electric network panel show where ratios fail.
Chests, storage tanks, and the logistic network's storage chests buffer items, and full outputs stall machines upstream.
Labs consume science packs of rising recipe complexity to research a technology graph that leads through oil processing, robots, and nuclear power to the rocket silo.
Straight and curved rail pieces are placed to build train networks, with elevated rails in Space Age, and the rail planner lays segments between points.
Trains run schedules of stations with wait conditions on cargo, time, inactivity, or circuit signals.
Space Age elevated rails let a second track layer cross over ground tracks and buildings.
Cows, sheep, pigs, chickens, horses, water buffalo, and goats with offspring need feed and care and yield products.
Dynamically generated contracts such as mowing, fertilizing, or hauling pay for work on other farmers' fields.
Fields move through cultivating or plowing, seeding, fertilizing, weeding, and harvesting with matching implements; 25 crop types follow seasonal calendars, with rice grown in paddies.
Hired AI helpers drive vehicles to work fields while the player does other tasks.
Bank loans fund early expansion.
ModHub distributes developer-tested community mods that add vehicles, maps, and scripts.
Productions and farm shops convert crops into processed goods as business ventures.
Twisters and hail can damage crops.
A seasonal cycle, introduced in FS22, sets planting and harvest windows.
Tires leave tracks that deform soft ground.
The player drives over 400 licensed vehicles and implements from more than 150 brands, each with its own power, speed, and weight; GPS-assisted steering automates straight passes.
Vehicles accumulate wear and damage that reduce performance until repaired at a workshop.
Rising prosperity draws stronger raiders and foreign armies; difficulty is adjustable and pacifist mode removes them.
Dysentery, cholera, tetanus, rabies, frostbite, and plague spread or strike based on water, clothing, rats, and healer coverage.
Twelve crops with rotation to preserve soil fertility; fields improve by clearing weeds and rocks and adjusting the soil mix.
Desirability from surroundings gates housing upgrades.
Nineteen food types; diet variety, including berries and greens against scurvy, is needed for health.
Housing and the town center advance through tiers as prosperity and desirability grow.
Palisades, stone walls, towers, barracks, and equipped soldiers.
A tree of over 140 points of upgrades.
Crafted goods are traded for resources the town lacks.
Player attributes develop through training schedules, match experience, and coaching quality up to individual potential.
Fixtures are simulated event by event from each player's attributes, condition, and morale and the manager's tactics and touchline instructions, shown in 2D or 3D.
The board sets season expectations and, with fan confidence, judges results against them; falling confidence brings warnings and then sacking.
Club finances cover wage and transfer budgets, with taxes added in FM 2013.
Press conferences pose questions with answer options that change morale and media relations.
Players peak and decline with age, retire, and are replaced by yearly youth intakes.
Transfer fees are negotiated with selling clubs and contracts with players and their agents over wages, length, bonuses, and clauses, and talks can break down.
Personality and hidden attributes such as professionalism affect development and reactions.
Generated youth players enter the database each season alongside the real ones.
Squad hierarchy, cohesion, and player opinions of the manager are tracked from FM 2018.
Club and manager reputation set who will sign; board and fan confidence decide whether the manager is sacked.
Players' attributes are shown only as well as the club's scouts know them; scout knowledge accumulates per region and is shown as a percentage from FM 2018.
Team talks and private conversations with players praise, criticize, or promise, changing morale.
Players and staff are signed through transfers, loans, and contracts with wages, bonuses, and agents.
Data analysts and statistics screens report player and team performance.
Buildings are placed and rotated without a grid.
Progress unlocks through tiers guided by a book, along Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates.
Buildings and monuments are assembled from individual parts whose choice sets function and appearance.
Trade with neighboring villages.
A painting tool marks areas for homes, roads, patrol routes, and forest extraction; homes fill residential zones organically.
Wildfires spread through vegetation and can be extinguished.
Powers such as jellifying water are granted by completing objectives; magical stones protect against water and fire.
Water flows over the terrain, erodes it, and floods low ground and villages; tsunamis sweep across islands.
Lava cools into solid rock, water erodes soil, fire burns vegetation, and powers can jellify or remove water.
Tsunamis and eruptions, announced shortly before by shamans.
Each map is cleared by settling every totem to open a portal.
The Breath picks up and deposits sand, water, and lava in real time to build land bridges, dams, and barriers.
Villagers are sent to totems to found villages.
Hope and Discontent meters respond to laws, events, and conditions; hope too low or discontent too high for too long ends the game in revolt.
Temperature falls on a schedule toward the Great Storm, which the main scenario must be survived through.
Citizens work daylight shifts; emergency shifts extend hours at a cost.
Individual decisions, such as how to handle an injured child, offer choices that shift hope and discontent.
Scouts explore the frozen wasteland map for survivors and resources, the only way to grow the workforce.
Workers, engineers, and children fill different job types.
The Book of Laws offers adaptation laws such as child labor, extended shifts, and prosthetics, plus Order or Faith paths whose later laws are harsher.
Coal, wood, steel, and food come from thumpers, sawmills, mines, and hunters.
The generator heats a circular area whose range and level the player raises; buildings outside heat need insulation or heaters.
Workshops research heat, extraction, and automaton technologies.
Whiteouts are severe storms prepared for with fuel reserves.
A council of 100 faction delegates votes on each proposed law; 51 votes pass most laws, two thirds pass laws that grant the Steward more power.
Factions with conflicting ideals react to adopted ideas and laws; radicals grow within factions.
Laws are proposed, negotiated with promises, and enacted when the council approves.
Food, coal, oil, and steam come from frostland deposits and districts.
Utopia Builder mode sets an objective and optional challenges that fail the run if missed.
Faction tension can escalate into murder and civil war.
An Idea Tree of faction-proposed ideas to solve problems.
Districts for food, housing, extraction, and industry are placed on frost; buildings inside add functions.
Crew gain skill in piloting, engines, shields, weapons, repair, and combat through use, improving station bonuses.
Each jump advances the rebel fleet across the sector map; overtaken beacons yield hard fights and no reward, forcing a trade between exploration and speed.
Hits and events start fires that spread between rooms, damage systems and crew, and burn oxygen; crew extinguish them or the player vents the room.
Each room has an oxygen level that equalizes through open doors, drains through hull breaches and opened airlocks, and is refilled by the oxygen system; crew suffocate in empty rooms.
Beacon contents are unknown until visited unless revealed by upgrades such as long-range scanners.
Losing the ship or all crew ends the run and deletes the save; dead crew members are gone.
Eight species have fixed traits such as faster repair, fire immunity, or extra combat damage.

Reactor power bars are assigned among shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, medbay, and other systems, usually while paused in combat; each system caps how many bars it accepts, and damage removes usable bars until crew repair it.
Each sector is a generated map of about twenty beacons with stores, hazards, and events.
Each weapon shot rolls against the target's evasion, shield layers absorb hits, and hits damage the room and the system inside it.

Hits damage the system in the struck room (shields, weapons, engines, oxygen, piloting), removing its usable power bars until crew repair it, and the player targets enemy rooms to disable specific systems.
Beacon events offer text choices, with extra options unlocked by specific crew, systems, or equipment, and some quests chain across beacons.
The player moves crew between rooms to man stations, repair systems and breaches, fight boarders, and put out fires; crew act on their own only within the room they occupy.
Pause is the main tactical tool for issuing orders mid-combat.
Marketing campaigns bought during development raise a game's hype, which boosts its launch sales.
Staff gain experience and can be sent to training to raise stats or specialize.
Salaries, office upkeep, and development costs drain cash between releases; running out ends the game.
Fictional consoles launch and retire on a fixed in-game calendar from the 1980s onward, so platform choice is a bet on a console's remaining market life.
Bigger offices, R&D and hardware labs, and larger projects unlock as money and fans grow.
Mods are written in JavaScript through the gdt-modAPI and shared on the Steam Workshop.
Each game is a topic, genre, platform, and audience pick plus focus sliders across three development stages; reviews score its fit and quality against the studio's best.
A fan count from past releases scales sales of future games.
After moving out of the garage, the player hires designers and programmers with design, technology, and speed stats and assigns them to development tasks.
Research points unlock new topics, genres, and engine features; custom engines bundle researched features and raise technology output.
Industry news, console launches, and studio events fire on a fixed historical timeline.
The player's only act is toggling cells on the grid to set the seed before running generations.
Each generation is a discrete synchronous update the player can step through one at a time.
Computer implementations step one generation at a time or run continuously; later simulators such as Golly use Hashlife to jump far ahead in time.
The duplicator tool and Advanced Duplicator addon copy and paste multi-prop contraptions.
Steam Workshop distributes saves, dupes, maps, and addons.
The player is a first-person character who walks, flies with noclip, and wields the physics and tool guns.
A Lua API covers entities, weapons, HUD, and game rules; servers send addons to clients on join, and community game modes (TTT, Prop Hunt, DarkRP) became the main way people play.
The tool gun joins props with welds, ropes, axles, sliders, winches, motors, wheels, and thrusters, turning loose props into vehicles and machines.
Every spawned prop and ragdoll is a physics object; the physics gun lifts, rotates, and freezes them, and collisions, gravity, and buoyancy follow the Source physics engine.
The Wiremod addon adds wires, sensors, gates, and programmable chips to contraptions.
Researchers interview agents and read their memory streams to evaluate believability.
Each morning the model drafts a day plan of about five to eight broad chunks, decomposed into hour-long and then 5-15 minute actions that agents revise when they react to events.
Plans, dialogue, importance ratings, and reflections are all generated by gpt-3.5-turbo calls at runtime.

Information spreads only through agent conversations; over two game days awareness of a mayoral candidacy rose from 1 to 8 agents and of a party from 1 to 13, with 6 of 453 awareness answers hallucinated.
