Each agent's memory stream stores observations, plans, and reflections as text; retrieval ranks them by recency (0.995 decay per game hour), model-rated importance (1-10), and embedding relevance, and reflections fire when summed importance exceeds 150.
Users address agents in natural language as a persona or as the agent's inner voice, and can rewrite the status of objects in natural language.
Agents form acquaintances through conversation; network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74 over two game days.
Skills such as Animal Handling improve through use, including hunting and combat.
Settlers in poor conditions become dissatisfied and may leave the settlement.
Settlers track needs such as hunger, sleep, clothing preferences, and religion, and meeting them keeps settlers content.
Backgrounds, traits, and perks set at settler creation.
Repeated bandit raids and animal attacks are met with walls, traps, and settlers equipped and commanded in battle.
Workshops, chapels, libraries, and bedrooms are furnished and decorated rooms.
Seasonal changes govern food production and storage.
Food keeps longer in cool storage such as cellars.
Built structures need support, and unsupported sections collapse.
Research unlocks medieval technology.
A 3D terrain toolset digs out or fills voxel earth and water on a randomly generated multi-level map, so cellars, moats, and caverns are carved from the ground.
Settlements stack multi-storey buildings above ground and cellars and caverns below, connected by stairs and ladders.
Settlers are assigned to roles that fit their skills.
Simulation mode requires earning driver's licenses through timed tests before entering higher events.
Credits and prize cars build a garage drawn from 140 production cars.
The first game designed for DualShock analog control and rumble; license tests and races grade precise braking and cornering.
Credits buy performance parts and tuning that tailor a car to the player's driving style.
Championships award trophies, credits, and prize cars.
Each of 140 cars has its own handling that responds to parts and tuning; reviewers rated it above any earlier racing game.
Racing lines, braking points, and throttle control on wheel or pad decide results; GT Sophy is trained to the same physics.
Tire, suspension, aerodynamics, and drivetrain models per car; tuning parts and settings change handling.
Each round opens with a steward's report of births, deaths, harvest, rat losses, and land price.
Planted acres consume seed grain and return a random yield per acre at year end; each person can farm only a set amount of land, so labor caps planting.
People must be fed grain each year; if at least 45 percent starve in one round the game ends early.
Each year carries a chance of plague that halves the population.
Rats eat a random amount of stored grain each year, a loss on holding stock.
Ten rounds, each one year: a status report, then three typed decisions (acres to buy or sell, bushels to feed, acres to plant) before the year resolves.
Shifts are timed; Open Shift mode removes the limit.
Rooms hold atmosphere, and an uncontrolled decompression flushes the player and loose objects out of the ship.
The character owes $1.2 billion to Lynx Corporation, and salvage earnings pay it down.

Systems must be made safe in order: pressurized rooms vented, electrical and coolant lines avoided, and reactors delivered before they melt down; mistakes produce the physical result rather than an error.
Ships are assemblies of separable parts; freed parts keep mass and momentum in zero gravity and are pulled or flung with the tether grapple toward the right receptacle.
The laser cutter severs structure at cut points and joints; cutting live electrical wires or coolant pipes can cause an explosion, so where and in what order to cut is the core decision.
Oxygen and thruster fuel deplete during a shift and must be replenished.
Chickens must be fed and kept indoors or they can die; cows need daily feed, talking, brushing, and milking, and fall sick or die if neglected.
Crops need water every day; a missed day halts growth rather than killing the plant, and each crop belongs to a season.
A stamina pool limits work each day; power berries found around the map raise it.
After dark only the bar stays open, so shopping and visits must fit daylight.
Villagers' and candidates' affection rises with talking and gifts.
Five eligible women can be courted; marriage and a child count toward the final evaluation.
After two and a half years the father evaluates the farm, family, and relationships.
A four-season calendar sets which crops can grow and when festivals occur.
The player draws front lines and offensive arrows for armies under generals, and the AI moves divisions to carry out the battle plan; divisions can also be ordered directly.
Countries join factions and guarantee others; world tension from 0 to 100 gates what democracies can do.

Division templates combine battalions (infantry, tanks, cavalry, motorized, mechanized) and support companies, and the mix sets combat statistics and equipment needs; tank, ship, and plane designers added by DLC apply the same idea to equipment.
Mobilization, conscription, and trade laws and ministers are bought with political power.
Political power accrues over time and is spent on laws such as mobilization, conscription, and trade, on ministers, and on decisions.
Military factories turn strategic resources into equipment on production lines, dockyards build ships, and civilian factories build infrastructure and handle trade.
Ideology popularity among democratic, communist, fascist, and non-aligned groups shifts the government and can end in civil war.
Divisions fight in hourly combat rounds comparing attacks against defense or breakthrough, draining organization and strength under terrain, weather, and supply modifiers.

Supply hubs connect to the capital by railway, with hub capacity set by railway level and limited by the weakest link; supply falls off per province from the hub, and divisions at 35% supply or less suffer attrition and combat penalties.

Research runs in parallel slots, and each country has a national focus tree in which one focus at a time is completed for bonuses such as extra factories or events; at launch only Germany, the UK, the USSR, and the US had unique trees.
States are core or non-core, armies occupy enemy states during war, and peace conferences transfer ownership.
When a country capitulates, winners take turns spending peace conference points on annexation, puppets, and other demands.
Sea and air regions have weather that affects operations.
Using tools earns experience that is spent on tool upgrades that speed up work.
Sales are resolved by buyers bidding at auction.
Neighbors send email jobs (cleaning, painting, installing heaters, showers, or air conditioners, furnishing) whose pay depends on job size and quality.
Each property has potential buyers with different needs, such as cleanliness or a family room, who bid according to how well the renovated house suits them.
Furniture, doors, windows, and wallpaper from a catalog are placed freely.
Paint roller, mop, window cleaner, and plaster tool apply coverage to walls, floors, and windows with visible progress; tiling and demolition use the same direct tool loop.
Players accumulate discovered elements and First Discoveries, which mark elements no player had made before.
Every action combines two owned elements; on a cache miss a Llama model names the result, the result is stored so every player gets the same answer, and new results earn a First Discovery label.
On a cache miss, a Llama model generates the combined element's name (up to twenty tokens) and emoji; the result is written to a shared database so later requests are deterministic.
Careers include active jobs played on site.
The developers list disease, alongside rumors and trends, among the outcomes that spread through Zois' autonomous interactions.
Canvas is the in-game platform for sharing characters, homes, and stories.
Players can switch from point-and-click orders to direct control of a Zoi or a vehicle.
Build mode places walls, roofs, stairs, fences, and gates; city edit changes streets, properties, and weather.
Text prompts generate patterns and images for outfits, props, and furniture; 2D images become 3D in-game objects; uploaded video becomes character motion.
Autonomous interactions generate rumors that spread among Zois.
Zois age and die.
An on-device small language model lets the player type prompts that influence a Zoi's thoughts and actions.
Eight needs (hunger, hygiene, bathroom, fun, social, energy, sleep, recognition) decay and drive Zois' free-will choices.

City-wide free will keeps Zois across the city living autonomously while the player directs one household, producing rumors, trends, and disease; the fidelity of the update for distant Zois is not documented.
Personality and life experience shape each Zoi's actions and relationships.
Licenses progress Rookie, D, C, B, A, with Pro for esports qualifiers; promotion depends on a per-discipline Safety Rating computed from incident points and corners per incident.
Races are against human drivers on the publisher's servers, so results depend on the driver's braking, throttle, and line precision.
A new tire model replaced the one in the NASCAR Racing 2003 Season code iRacing was built from, and cars and tracks are LIDAR-scanned.
Cars take damage and tires wear over a race, which pit stops address.
Each building scores points from nearby compatible buildings and natural features and loses points for incompatible ones; the preview shows the total before placing.
Buildings are placed freely on the island and cannot be removed or built over.
Reaching a point threshold restocks the inventory and offers a choice of two building packs; filling the gauge unlocks a new island.
Each island is procedurally generated.
The player's tracked head and hands are the avatar at a room-scale workstation; a smaller human mode adjusts reach.
Most objects within reach can be picked up and manipulated with tracked controllers, fixed appliances expose buttons, levers, and dials, and post-game modifiers change the physics.
Four jobs (Office Worker, Gourmet Chef, Store Clerk, Auto Mechanic) each run a sequence of task requests from job bots.
Diseases spread among dinosaurs and must be treated by rangers or ACU.
Each division offers contracts with requirements and rewards that unlock research and story missions.
Guests want viewing of varied species plus shopping, food, and amenities, and flee or die during breakouts.
The player can drive ranger jeeps and ACU helicopters to resupply feeders, repair fences, and tranquilize dinosaurs.
Island star ratings unlock the next island in the Las Cinco Muertes archipelago.
Dinosaurs have feeding and social needs plus grassland, forest, and population limits; unmet needs lower comfort, and carnivores hunt herbivores and attack fences and guests.
Facilities need power from plants through substations; outages open electric fences.
Storms damage fences and power and set dinosaurs loose; breakouts must be contained before guests are hurt.
Science, Security, and Entertainment divisions track reputation; low standing in one triggers sabotage such as power cuts or disease outbreaks.
The Expedition Center sends teams to global dig sites that yield fossils for DNA and for sale.
Fossil DNA completion unlocks species, and the research center unlocks buildings, upgrades, and genome modifications.
Skills rise from the actions they describe, such as stealing for thievery and fighting for combat, with stats and appearance changing as characters grow.
Zone soil types and terrain affect outpost farming.
Many factions and species with relations to each other; the player can aid or oppose them, and deaths of notable figures shift world states.
Outposts are built and upgraded into fortified havens or businesses.
Each limb has its own health; limbs can be damaged or severed and replaced with prosthetic or robotic limbs, and blood loss and injuries reduce stats and movement while squadmates carry the wounded.
Outposts must be defended against attackers.
Player standing with each faction changes access and hostility.
Fights resolve from character combat skills, weapon stats, and armor, with damage applied to individual limbs.
Starvation reduces character stats.
Research unlocks equipment and technologies.
The player commands any squad member directly in real time with pause; no character is privileged, and the squad acts together.
Some weather, such as acid rain, harms characters.
Squad members keep job lists for base work and production.
Career funds pay for parts, fuel, crew, and facility upgrades; contract payouts are the income.
Career contracts pay for objectives such as reaching an orbit or testing a part, with deadlines and penalties.
Manual ascents, landings, and docking reward piloting skill; SAS assists attitude hold.
Drag, lift, and control surfaces govern ascent profiles, spaceplanes, and aerobraking.
Atmospheric entry heats parts; heat shields absorb it and overheated parts are destroyed.
C# plugins and part configs extend the game; mods such as Real Solar System and Principia replace the planetary system and the orbital model.

Craft are built in the Vehicle Assembly Building or Spaceplane Hangar from pods, tanks, engines, decouplers, wings, and science parts; part order sets the staging sequence, and each stage's mass, thrust, and fuel set its delta-v.

Patched conics: a vessel orbits one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries; maneuver nodes preview delta-v and the resulting trajectory; planets ride fixed rails rather than n-body motion.
Kerbals die in crashes and EVA accidents; Career mode costs reputation for deaths, and a difficulty option sets whether lost crews respawn.
Career reputation rises with completed contracts and falls with failures and Kerbal deaths.
Drills mine ore on planets and asteroids that converters turn into fuel, a system adopted from mods.
Each part is a rigid body joined to its parent with a joint of limited strength; excess force breaks joints, so tall stacks wobble and hard impacts shed parts or kill Kerbals.
Parts are destroyed individually by impact or overheating, removing their engines, tanks, or controls from the craft.
Science from experiments unlocks part nodes in Science and Career modes.
On-rails time warp skips long coasts; physics warp speeds powered flight at reduced stability.
Happiness from layout, churches, taverns, and festivals.
Plagues spread and must be healed.
Diplomats make trade agreements, alliances, and wars with AI kingdoms.
Happiness and housing attract new residents.
Castle blocks stack into walls and towers whose shape forms automatically; taller archer towers have longer range.
Vikings kidnap peasants, steal resources, and burn the town; dragons torch granaries; ogres attack; soldiers and archer towers defend.
Lightning starts fires.
Foresters cut and replant trees.
An annual winter destroys crops, so food must be stored in granaries to prevent starvation.
Peasant taxes pay workers and unlock buildings.
Advertising signs bought each day raise that day's demand alongside price and weather, with no carryover between days.
Cash on hand limits how many glasses and signs can be bought each day.
Aggregate customers buy more at lower prices and with more advertising signs; sales are capped by the glasses made that day.
The weather for the day is shown before the player commits to production.
Thunderstorms void a day's profits; street closures and blown-away signs also occur.
Twelve rounds of one day each: the player makes decisions, the day resolves, and an earnings report follows.
Each day is sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry, and the weather sets the demand level the price and sign choices act on.
Keyboard commands deliver food (CTRL+F), add water to his tank (CTRL+W), deliver dog food, pat him, or give records and books; a resident left unfed turns green and sick until he eats.
He runs a routine of cooking, watching television, reading the newspaper, playing records, and dancing on a compressed day of about six real-time hours.
Typed requests such as 'Please play piano' are matched against a keyword vocabulary; politeness helps, and a sad or sick resident may refuse.
Hunger and thirst build between deliveries; unmet needs lower his mood and eventually make him visibly sick.
Seeded personality and mood parameters change which activities he prefers, how often he invites the player to cards or writes letters, and how readily he obeys.
The disk serial number seeds his name from a pool of 256, his shirt color, personality, and behavior parameters.
Approval responds to supply, taxes, and tithes.
Fields depend on soil fertility per crop; rotation and fallow maintain yields, and overuse exhausts soil.
Households need basic goods and luxuries; shortfalls lower satisfaction.
Raw materials pass through workshops into goods, weapons, and armor.
Bandit raids threaten the town and loot stores.
Hunting grounds depend on animal populations; overexpansion drives deer away and deforests land.
Roads curve freely and plots and buildings take their shape from them.
Spring rains and winter snow change work and needs.
Six tax types, a yearly King's tax, and tithes on villagers.
Surpluses sold to traveling merchants; imports and exports balanced through trade.
Real-time battles with fatigue, weather, and equipment; retinue, mercenaries, and militia drawn from townspeople.
Residential plots drawn along roads are divided into burgage plots that families build on and extend with backyard production.
The physics engine computes forces over more than 1,000 control surfaces and models wind flowing over terrain; a legacy flight model option remains.
An in-game marketplace and third-party aircraft and airports extend the sim.

The whole Earth is built from Bing Maps imagery updated every 28 days and AI-generated 3D content streamed from more than two petabytes in the cloud, while Meteoblue live weather and live air traffic feed the sim at runtime.
Meteoblue live global weather sets clouds, wind, and precipitation in real time, and wind interacts with the terrain model.
Starting from an airport the player chooses, experience earns certifications and specializations that unlock job types.
Career jobs include aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, Beluga outsize cargo, A400M arctic cargo, and airline passenger flights.
The pilot walks around the aircraft on foot during preflight.
Aircraft physics were revised, and ground contact models 3D stones, gravel, and grass that affect wheels during takeoff, landing, and taxi.
A walk-around preflight handles covers, doors, and service items, and revised electrical, fuel, pneumatic, and hydraulic systems gate start-up.
The streamed whole-Earth world of the 2020 game continues, and the launch showed the dependence when an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.
Career reputation accumulates alongside experience.
Survival maps send progressively stronger waves with tougher unit types and bosses as wave numbers rise; the cited sources do not tie wave strength to the player's own wealth.
Schematics save layouts as shareable text and are traded on Steam Workshop.
Conveyors, junctions, routers, sorters, overflow gates, and bridges move items from drills to the core, factories, and turret ammo inputs.
A visible timer counts down to the next wave, and wave timing can be changed in custom game rules.
Conduits carry water, slag, oil, and cryofluid; optional coolant and lubricant raise turret and factory rates.
Optional coolant and lubricant fed to turrets and factories raise their rates, and water boosts drill speed.
The GPL-3.0 source allows unrestricted mods, and community servers run plugins for custom maps and game modes.

Micro, logic, and hyper processors run Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language with one operation per instruction that reads sensors and memory cells, controls linked buildings and turrets, and binds units with ubind to command them.
Combustion, steam, solar, thorium, and impact generators feed node-linked grids with batteries; turrets, shields, and factories draw power.
Smelters, presses, kilns, separators, and mixers turn copper, lead, sand, coal, titanium, and thorium into graphite, silicon, plastanium, and surge alloy.
Enemy waves spawn on a schedule and path toward the core; about 18 Serpulo and 10 Erekir turret types consume ammo items, liquids, or power, backed by walls, menders, and shield projectors.
Mechanical, pneumatic, laser, and airblast drills mine ore tiles at speeds set by drill tier and ore hardness, with optional water boosting.
Campaign sectors set win conditions such as surviving a number of waves or destroying enemy cores on attack maps.
Over 250 technology blocks are researched by spending core resources along a tree that also gates campaign sectors.
Since version 7 units can be selected and commanded RTS-style, while others follow default AI or logic control.
Passive mobs breed when fed their preferred food and yield food, wool, and leather.
Crops grow in stages on farmland, faster with water nearby and light.
A 20-minute real-time day; hostile mobs spawn in low light, so night and caves are dangerous, and beds skip the night.
Fire spreads to nearby flammable blocks such as wood and wool and burns them away.
Water and lava flow a limited number of blocks out from source blocks; where they meet they form cobblestone, stone, or obsidian.
Any block can be placed on the voxel grid, so building has no fixed footprint.
A 2x2 inventory grid and a 3x3 crafting table turn blocks and items into tools, armor, and blocks from shaped recipes; furnaces, anvils, and enchanting tables extend the recipe set.
On death in survival the player's inventory and some experience drop at the death site and despawn after a few minutes if not recovered.
Java Edition mods (Forge, Fabric) and Bedrock add-ons, datapacks, and server plugins are widely used.
Public multiplayer servers and Realms host worlds that persist for many players.
Worlds generate from a seed into biomes, caves, ravines, villages, and ore layers that vary by depth; terrain extends effectively without limit in horizontal directions.
Blocks are mined by hand or with tools whose tier (wood, stone, iron, diamond, netherite) sets mining speed and which ores drop items.
Redstone dust carries power from levers, buttons, and sensors through repeaters and comparators to pistons, doors, and dispensers.
Survival mode has health and hunger bars; food restores hunger, high hunger regenerates health, and starvation, falls, drowning, and mobs deal damage.
Material tiers gate progression: iron tools mine diamonds, diamond tools mine obsidian, and Nether materials gate brewing and the End.
Passengers ride to any station of their target shape, transferring between lines when needed.
Each in-game week grants extra rolling stock and a choice of assets such as tunnels, bridges, new lines, or interchanges.
The player draws colored lines between stations and assigns trains that load and unload automatically; ridership is the score.
Passengers wait at stations with limited capacity, typically six; interchanges raise capacity and loading speed, and a station overcrowded too long ends the game.
Time can be paused to reroute lines or move trains.
Races are simulated in real time from driver attributes, car part performance, tyres, fuel, and weather, with the player intervening on strategy.
The chairman sets objectives each season, and missing them lowers the chairman's confidence until the player is fired.
Prize money and sponsor income fund salaries and part development.
Car parts are designed and built over time, rated on performance, and chosen for next season's car, which sets pace at pre-season testing.
Driver and staff contracts are negotiated over wages, length, and bonuses, and candidates can reject offers and end talks.
Drivers have distinct personality types that cause team drama and respond differently to tough love or support.
Drivers, team managers, mechanics, and designers are hired; skilled mechanics shorten pit stops.
Races run in real time with pause and speed controls.
Tyres wear over a stint and car parts lose condition, so strategy balances pace against wear.
Dynamic weather during sessions forces calls such as switching to intermediates or staying on slicks.
Plots grouped with others producing the same resource get a production bonus.
Each round resources trade in a real-time auction: sellers and buyers walk avatars toward a price line, trades fire when they meet, and ties go to the trailing player.
Players walk a colonist through town to buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and lead them to plots under a turn timer.
Each player needs food and energy each round; low food shortens the next development turn and low energy stops some plots.
The store turns smithore into new M.U.L.E.s; with no smithore it cannot build more.
Sunspots, pirate raids, meteorites, and runaway M.U.L.E.s, targeted away from the last-place player.
A M.U.L.E. outfitted for food, energy, smithore, or crystite harvests its plot each round; output depends on terrain and the plot's development.
Computer opponents fill empty seats and compete for plots and auction trades.
Store prices respond to supply: refusing to sell raises a resource's price in later rounds, and smithore scarcity raises the price of new M.U.L.E.s.
Rounds run in fixed phases: land grant, timed development, production, then auctions for each resource.
Bark Mode lets nearby DS owners meet each other's dogs and exchange presents.
Touch petting, brushing, and washing plus food and water bowls maintain hunger, thirst, and coat condition; walks, balls, discs, and toys add play.
When the dog strikes a pose such as sit, the player records a spoken command; repeating the pairing teaches the trick, and the dog later responds to the voice cue.
Trial prize money and trainer points unlock new breeds and supplies.
The microphone recognizes the dog's name and trick words by matching the player's voice against recorded samples.
Hunger, thirst, and dirtiness worsen with real elapsed time.
Care state advances with the DS internal clock and calendar.
Each world seed defines two secret alchemy recipes (Lively Concoction and Alchemic Precursor), each made from three materials that players must find by experiment.
The player controls one witch with levitation, kicking, and wand casting.
Every pixel of terrain is a material that falls, flows, or rises by local rules, so digging, explosions, and spills reshape the level in real time.
Fire spreads through wood, grass, oil, and gunpowder and burns the player and enemies alike.
Liquids pool and flow and gases rise and spread through caves at pixel level.
Materials react by rule: lava and water form rock and steam, wood burns into smoke, acid eats terrain, and alchemical liquids such as polymorphine or teleportatium apply their effects on contact.
Lua-based mods are supported and distributed through Steam Workshop.
Wands have stats such as capacity, mana, recharge, and cast delay; spells and modifiers placed in a wand's slots execute in order, so arrangement changes what the wand does.
A death ends the run and the world is regenerated; only some unlocks, such as new spells in the pool, persist.
Each seed generates biome layouts from hand-made tile pieces within a fixed order of biomes.
Box2D rigid bodies such as crates, bricks, and detached terrain chunks can be kicked, thrown, and shattered.
Some resource tiles and patents are sold by auction.
Players buy shares in rival companies and win by holding a majority of every company; debt lowers stock price, and buying back one's own stock raises buyout cost.
Each HQ consumes life support resources such as water, food, oxygen, and power, which must be produced or bought.
Companies can run into debt, which depresses their share price.
Each match generates a new Martian map, so resource layouts and claims differ.
Steel mills, glass kilns, electronics factories, greenhouses, and hydrolysis reactors turn raw resources into higher-value goods and life support.
Extractors on claimed hex tiles mine water, aluminum, iron, silicon, and carbon at rates set by tile richness.
Up to eight companies, AI or human, compete in one market and attack each other through black market sabotage such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies.
Each of 13 resources has a market price that falls when players sell and rises when they buy, with shortages and gluts driving rapid swings.
Patents and HQ upgrades unlock buildings and bonuses.
Cost, cycles, and area are shown on histograms of all players' scores and against friends' scores; Zachtronics deliberately attaches no rewards to optimization.
A puzzle editor publishes solvable user puzzles to Steam Workshop, curated puzzles appear in the Journal of Alchemical Engineering, and solutions export as looping GIFs.
Solutions are scored on cost in gold, cycles to complete, and area in hex tiles, with the community adding an unofficial sum metric.

A machine is assembled from arms, extendable arms, tracks, and glyphs of bonding, unbonding, calcification, and projection, plus devices such as Van Berlo's wheel, with no limit on parts beyond their cost.
Each arm has a row on a shared instruction timeline of grab, drop, rotate, pivot, extend, retract, and track moves; the machine loops the program until the required number of products is output.
Each puzzle fixes the input reagents and the required product molecule; chapters must be completed to advance.
Dead party members are gone; the 1985 version leaves a tombstone with an epitaph.
Each round closes with one or two random events and weather, such as storms, wagon breakdowns, snakebites, or attacks, that cost supplies or health.
Food, clothing, and medical supplies are stocks drawn down each round at a player-chosen consumption rate; low food, cold without clothing, and untreated illness kill the traveler.
The trip is a sequence of two-week rounds with fixed phases: stop at a fort or not, hunt or not, set consumption, then travel and resolve events.
Weather each round affects travel and illness.
Player ratings develop and decline over careers, including fielding development added in OOTP 14.
Games are simulated pitch by pitch from batter, pitcher, and fielder ratings and managerial settings, in real time, pitch-by-pitch control, or bulk simulation.
Owners set expectations, and the general manager's job security falls when results and finances miss them, ending in dismissal.
Franchise finances cover payroll, revenue, and budgets; the system was reworked in OOTP 16.
League histories, records, and player careers are stored and exported as HTML reports.
Players age, retire, and are replaced by drafts and historical debuts.

Contract offers to free agents and extensions to rostered players are accepted or rejected against each player's demands, and trades are proposed to AI general managers who accept, reject, or counter.
Fictional players are generated for fictional leagues and amateur drafts.
Player ratings are shown through a scout's evaluation, so accuracy depends on the scouting staff; the system was recoded in OOTP 14.
The GM signs free agents, drafts amateurs, and hires managers, coaches, and scouts within a budget.
Extensive statistics and reports cover every player, team, and season.
Skill points are spent on skills, which raise morale expectations.
Critters are ranched for food and for their conversion of inputs into useful outputs.
Machines and duplicants emit polluted water, polluted oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat; a natural gas generator consumes 90 g/s of gas for 800 W and outputs 67.5 g/s polluted water and 22.5 g/s CO2.
Germs live on tiles, items, gases, and liquids; exposure past per-germ thresholds gives a contraction chance of 0.5 - 0.5 x tanh(resistance / 4).
Plants need specific temperatures, atmospheres, and irrigation.
Oxygen, temperature, power, plumbing, and germ overlays show hidden cell state.
Decor around a duplicant is compared to its recent average and feeds morale.
Dig, build, mop, and deconstruct orders placed on tiles.

Every tile holds one gas, liquid, or solid with a mass; gases diffuse and equalize when a chamber is opened, and liquids drain under gravity, so breathable oxygen must be produced and carbon dioxide managed.
Gas and liquid pipes carry packets between buildings; a liquid pipe segment holds 10 kg and moves packets once per second, capping a line at 10 kg/s, and pipe contents exchange heat with their tiles.

Cells exchange heat each 0.2 s tick with q = dT x dt x k x 1000, with multipliers for solid-gas and liquid-liquid contact; insulated tiles divide conductivity, and temperature thresholds melt, freeze, boil, or damage things.

Morale is the sum of timed buffs (Mess Hall +3, Private Bedroom +3, food up to +16, decor up to +12) compared to an expectation that rises with skills learned; each point under adds 2.5% stress per cycle up to 25%, full stress triggers a stress response, and 8 or more points over can trigger overjoyed responses.
Traits such as Germ Resistant or Allergies change resistances and stress reactions.
Coal, hydrogen, natural gas, and manual generators on wires and batteries; overloaded circuits take damage.
Asteroids are procedurally generated.
Enclosed rooms that meet requirements become Mess Halls, Bedrooms, and similar rooms that grant morale buffs.
Automation wires, sensors, and logic gates control doors, pumps, and generators; extended by the Automation Innovation update.
Food rots unless refrigerated or kept in a sterile atmosphere.
Research unlocks buildings.
Every errand carries a priority, and each duplicant has per-errand-type priorities on the Priorities screen; duplicants pick the highest available errand and favor tasks they are good at.
The end-of-day ledger adds wages and bribes, subtracts citation penalties, and requires paying rent, food, heat, and other necessities; going into debt ends the game.
Each shift is a fixed real-time working day and pay is per properly processed entrant, so processing speed trades against error risk.
Scripted entrants pose choices such as admitting a supposed spouse without complete papers, trading rule compliance against helping people.
Family members' condition worsens on days when food, heat, or other necessities go unpaid.
Randomly generated entrants are mixed with scripted ones; the unlockable endless mode uses only generated entrants.

Each day adds or changes entry requirements; the player cross-checks passports, permits, and other papers, can interrogate, compare fingerprints, or order body scans, and receives faxed citations after protocol violations.
EZIC contacts and other scripted encounters branch the story toward twenty endings, including escape to Obristan.
Jobs with flexible career progression paths.
Steam Workshop distributes community houses, Parafolks, and mods.
Grid-less building with curved walls, split-level floors, and resizable, recolorable, stackable furniture; walls are drawn with a road-style tool modeled on Cities: Skylines.
An in-game modding interface lets players edit or add content.
Parafolks carry needs, wants, and emotions that steer their autonomous behavior and set the player's care tasks.
Conversation fills a together bar between two Parafolks, and a full bar unlocks together cards.
Monthly rent and electricity bills must be paid or the player incurs debt.
Customer requests, discount alerts, spam, and scams arrive in an inbox; accepted orders left unfulfilled are rejected, and timed jobs grow more common as the career advances.
3DMark benchmarking scores built or repaired machines.
Email jobs ask for virus removal, upgrades, fixes, or overclocking on customer PCs; the player opens the case, identifies the faulty or missing part, and swaps it.
Leveling up from job experience unlocks more advanced parts.
PCs are assembled from licensed cases, motherboards, CPUs, coolers, GPUs, memory, and storage; part choice and installation details such as thermal paste decide whether and how well the machine runs.
Floodplain and meadow farms yield by fertility and season.
Houses need food and goods to advance.
A yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms; irrigation ditches extend fertile land, and Osiris can raise or lower the flood quality.
Buildings and monument crews draw workers from housing.
Monuments such as pyramids need delivered materials and worker crews over in-game years, and many missions require completing them.
Housing improves in level when demands for goods, services, and surroundings are met.
Missions set population, rating, and monument goals.
The flood season fixes when floodplain land can be farmed.
Raw materials and goods trade with other cities for money.
Fire marshals, constables, and other service walkers roam roads from their buildings and cover the houses they pass.

Infection spreads within countries and between them along travel links, at rates set by the pathogen's transmission traits and each country's conditions, until countries are fully infected and then depopulated.
Once the disease is noticed, countries fund cure research shown as a global progress bar; finishing it ends the run, so the player races to kill before it fills.
Hot, cold, and other national conditions slow a pathogen that lacks the matching resistance evolutions.
The Evolved scenario creator builds custom plagues, worlds, and events, with over 10,000 shared on Steam Workshop.
Evolved ships 23 scenarios and 10 disease types, each with altered rules.
DNA points buy nodes in three trees (transmission, symptoms, abilities); symptoms raise severity and lethality, and abilities resist climate and drugs.
Any selection of pieces can be saved as a blueprint and placed again.
Coasters, scenery blueprints, and parks are uploaded to and downloaded from the Steam Workshop or Frontier Workshop.
Thousands of guests with individual needs, preferences, and budgets choose rides and shops and show thoughts about prices and park conditions.
Ticket, ride, and shop prices are weighed against ride ratings and guest budgets.
Scenery around rides and paths raises guest happiness and ride appeal.
Coasters are test-run and rated on excitement, fear, and nausea, which set guest demand and ride value.
Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, and structures are assembled from modular wall, roof, and prop pieces.
Guests need food, drink, toilets, and rest during their visit.
Career scenarios set goals such as building coasters, reaching park ratings, and hiring staff; a scenario editor was added in 2017.
Janitors, mechanics, entertainers, vendors, and security guards are hired and assigned.
Challenge and Career modes gate rides and items behind research.
A voxel terrain editor sculpts and tunnels the ground.
Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, joining track elements end to end.
Rides age and break down without mechanic inspections.
Habitat and building blueprints are shared on the Steam Workshop.
Guests choose exhibits, shops, and talks and react to animal welfare and park layout.
Each species needs habitat size, land and water area, biome terrain and plants, temperature, shelter, and enrichment; welfare drops when any requirement is unmet.
Animals age from juveniles to adults and die of old age.
Barriers, buildings, and scenery use Planet Coaster's modular piece system.
Animals have food, water, social, enrichment, and privacy needs whose shortfalls lower welfare and can cause illness.
In Franchise mode an online animal market shared across players lists animals for sale and trade, priced in conservation credits.
A conservation rating rises with endangered species, releases to the wild, and education.
Keepers, vets, mechanics, security, and vendors are hired with work zones and facility needs.
Vets research species to unlock knowledge and enrichment items.
Animals carry genomes that set lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit them, and inbreeding causes harmful effects.
Sandbox designs are published as Workshop levels, and test runs export as GIF replays.
A level passes when its vehicles reach their flags; total material cost against the level budget is the measure of a good solution, and Steam leaderboards compare results.
Bridges are built from road, wood, steel, rope, cable, and hydraulic members connected at joints; materials trade cost against strength and weight.
Cars, trucks, and other vehicles are physics bodies whose mass and speed load the bridge.
Levels fix anchor points, allowed materials, budget, and vehicle routes.
A multi-phase hydraulics controller fires pistons when vehicles reach checkpoints.
Every member carries tension or compression shown as a stress color; a member past its material limit breaks and the load redistributes, often cascading into collapse.
Mana from the follower population unlocks progressively stronger interventions: knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods.
Landscape type changes how followers develop.
500 worlds, each won by defeating the enemy's followers.
Raising and lowering land is the basic power; its main use is creating flat ground on which followers can build larger settlements.
A papal magnet and behavior modes send followers to settle, gather, or fight.
Career mode in the town of Muckingham offers 38 main jobs plus bonus jobs whose pay buys upgrades and cosmetics.
Ladders and scaffolding reach higher surfaces.
Challenge mode limits water or time and ranks the result.

Four nozzles with different power and spray width and surface-specific soaps remove dirt, grime, lichen, moss, and rust; progress bars track each object and the level, and a button highlights remaining dirt.

Training courses and part-time jobs raise and lower her attributes; attributes gate jobs, decide October festival contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking against rival girls, and select the final career.
A small annual income pays for lessons, clothing, food, treatment, and shopping; jobs supplement it.
Eight years of scheduled training, jobs, and rest shape the daughter's attributes, and at 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings.
Repeating a part-time job leads to promotions, higher pay, and bonuses for unbroken success streaks.
Each month has three activity slots (early, middle, late), so every period spent training, working, adventuring, or resting is a period not spent on the others.
The daughter ages from 10 to 18; jobs and events unlock with age, and the game ends at 18.
Stress from work and training is relieved by free time, vacations, spa stays, or bed rest; poor rest management leads to illness and weaker performance.
Events and reactions fire on age, attributes, and season, leading into 74 career endings with retrospective sequences.
The month is the turn, split into three phases that resolve after the player sets the schedule.
Crowd flow through doors and corridors shapes congestion and fights.
Income per prisoner per day against staff wages and construction.
Player prisons are shared online, and Escape Mode lets players break out of shared prisons.
Federal grants pay out for meeting stated construction or program objectives.
Guards, dog handlers, armed guards, and snitches counter contraband, gangs, and escape attempts through patrols, searches, and lockdowns.

Hiring a Warden unlocks an hourly regime per risk category with Lockup, Sleep, Eat, Yard, Shower, Free Time, and Work blocks; each block confines prisoners to areas rather than forcing actions, so needs are met only where the current block lets prisoners go.
Fires spread through the prison and must be fought by firemen.
Water pumps and pipes supply showers and toilets.
The prison is drawn tile by tile: foundations, walls, doors, and objects are placed, then workmen build them, and room types are assigned to enclosed areas that contain required objects.

About 21 prisoner needs (bladder, food, sleep, hygiene, freedom, family, privacy, spirituality, and others) each charge from 1 to 10 and are reset by specific objects or activities; a need at 10 triggers its side effect, and reports color needs from green to red.
Five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, plus death row.
Generators and cables power doors, lights, and kitchens.
Needs left unmet for long periods make prisoners irritated, then likely to fight, attack staff, attempt escape, or riot, and violence spreads to nearby prisoners until guards restore order.
Staff such as guards, cooks, janitors, doctors, psychologists, and lawyers are hired individually, and administrators unlock features.
A bureaucracy research tree unlocked through administrative staff.

Each patient has a hidden diagnosis; doctors order examinations, lab tests, and equipment procedures that each reveal symptoms, symptom frequencies are tuned so one exam rarely settles a case, and treatment, hospitalization, or surgery follows.
The player lays foundations, walls, floor tiles, doors, and windows and places equipment for each department, or starts from prefabs.
A campaign and six challenge levels set goals; sandbox mode removes them.
The player hires and specializes doctors, nurses, lab staff, and janitors and manages their job satisfaction; the Hospital Services DLC adds staff training.
Doctor Mode (2019) lets the player choose exams, diagnoses, and treatments for individual doctors and their patients.

Constituents give feedback on a constitution, amendments are generated, agents vote, and the amended constitution is distributed on a fixed schedule (feedback at 300 s, vote at 420 s, distribution at 600 s).
Goal generation, talking, and the cognitive controller run on language-model calls, with GPT-4o as the base model in the strongest configuration.
Memes and a religion (Pastafarianism, seeded by 20 priests in one town) spread through agent conversations and travel; conversion was tracked by keyword use and had not saturated after two hours.
Agents gather and craft Minecraft items; a 49-agent group plateaued at about 320 unique items over four hours.
A memory module stores conversations, actions, and observations across short and long timescales.
A social-awareness module infers other agents' sentiment, and the paper compares perceived with true likeability.

Agents deposit a share of inventory into community chests every 120 seconds at the constitutional rate, starting at 20 percent; when amendments cut it to 5-10 percent, payments fell to about 9 percent.
Skills such as carpentry and cooking level from activities, and skill books and magazines speed or unlock progress.
Water and power shut off within about a month, forcing preparation.
A vision cone limits what the survivor sees.
Carpentry builds walls, barricades, and forts.
Weapons, tools, and barricades are crafted; Build 42 overhauled crafting.
Wounds such as scratches, lacerations, bites, and fractures are tracked per body part with bleeding and bandaging; zombie infection is spread by saliva and blood and is always fatal.
Full Lua modding through the Steam Workshop.
Death ends the character; a new survivor can start in the same world.
Occupation and positive or negative traits are chosen at character creation; occupation also sets spawn location.
A climate system with seasons changes gear needs.
Food rots, and refrigeration ends when power fails.
Zombies respond to sight and hearing, so noise from actions such as gunfire or breaking windows draws them toward the survivor, and hordes migrate.

Moodles for hunger, thirst, fatigue, endurance, panic, stress, boredom, unhappiness, temperature, wetness, pain, bleeding, and sickness each grow in severity and penalize combat, movement, carrying, or healing.
Vehicles have physics and part condition.
Past exchanges are stored as social history that later rules reference.
Traits and interests weight which rules apply to a character.
Directed social networks track how much each character likes, is attracted to, and respects each other character; exchanges and third parties' opinions move the values.
Each level sets social goals, such as getting two named characters to date.
Exchanges such as winking, being friendly, or being mean have preconditions; CiF rules decide whether the target accepts and update networks and statuses.
A character's volition for each exchange is scored from matching rules, and only exchanges it is inclined toward are offered, ranked by likelihood.
New locomotive types become available as the calendar advances through the eras, from early steam engines toward diesels.
Delivery revenue depends on cargo type, distance, and travel time, so fast trains earn more for passengers and mail.
A small stock market lets the player trade its own and rival stock; rivals use stock dealings to try to take over the player's railroad.
Track is laid on a square tile grid and up to 32 stations are placed; the first station gets the engine shop where trains are built.
Starting capital is half a loan; bonds raise more at interest rates tied to the economy.
Accounts settle in two-year periods across a century of play.
Industries consume delivered freight and produce new cargo; players can build additional industries.
Signal towers act as passing loops and control train movements on shared track.
AI railroad barons build competing lines and start rate wars over shared stations.
Depots, stations, and terminals draw cargo from progressively larger surrounding areas.
Stations supply and demand goods and passengers; under the complex economy cities accept only certain products, so routing follows demand.
Track is laid tile by tile across terrain whose slope and features add cost, linking up to 32 stations.
Players can take direct control of individual train movements.
Each train gets ordered stops and a consist of mail, passenger, and freight cars for nine commodity types; consists can be changed at any stop.

A monthly budget funds infrastructure, jobs, education, roads, and military spending; the more initiatives the player funds, the more corruption and inflation rise, and the Economist governor receives the whole budget annually.
Civilian initiatives raise popular support region by region, and stabilizing the country without letting insurgents take control is the goal.
Funding more civilian initiatives raises corruption and inflation, which erode what the monthly budget achieves; the governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.
A governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.
Each region has its own geography, and selectable governors such as the Economist and the Warlord change the rules.
An insurgency emerges partway through and contests regions against coalition forces; later, peace can be negotiated with insurgent leaders.
Random events interrupt plans and offer choices.

Advisers present cards that the player swipes left or right; each choice moves one or more of four meters (church, people, army, treasury), and the reign ends when any meter becomes completely full or completely empty.
When a king's reign ends, play continues with a new king; unlocked cards and some effects carry across reigns, and the in-game years keep advancing.
Completing tasks unlocks new cards.
Story cards chain across reigns, such as the Devil's visits in the years 666, 1332, and 1998.
Raid strength scales with colony wealth, number of colonists, and difficulty, so growth raises danger.
Drafting switches a colonist from self-assigned work to direct player control for combat or emergencies.
Bodies are hierarchies of parts with hit points, bleeding, infection, scars, and prosthetics that change capacities like moving and manipulation.
Every mood effect is an itemized thought with a source and expiry, visible in the needs tab.
Mood below trait-adjusted break thresholds triggers minor, major, or extreme mental breaks; high mood can grant inspirations.
Colonists track food, rest, recreation, comfort, beauty, and other needs whose levels feed mood.
Selectable storytellers (Cassandra, Phoebe, Randy) choose incidents using a threat budget derived from colony wealth and time since the last major event.
A work tab matrix sets 1-4 priorities per colonist per job type; colonists self-assign.

The marketing panel runs time-limited paid campaigns, such as park or ride advertising and free-entry or half-price vouchers, that raise guest arrivals or demand for a chosen ride or stall while they last.
Clicking a guest shows cash, needs, thoughts, and ride history.
Guests navigate the path network and can get lost in mazes of paths.
Guests have money, a preferred ride intensity, a nausea tolerance, and needs, and they report thoughts such as a ride being too intense or a price too high.
Guests compare ride and shop prices with ride value and their remaining cash; overpriced items show up as complaints in guest thoughts.
Scenery and trees improve guest views and ride appeal.
Each ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea from its track geometry, speeds, and g-forces; ratings set demand and fair price.
Parks start with a loan, such as $50,000 in Mega Park.
Coasters are built track piece by piece on a tile grid, choosing direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews.
Guests get hungry, thirsty, tired, and need toilets during a visit.
Each of 21 base scenarios sets a goal such as a guest count with a minimum park rating by a deadline; completing one unlocks the next.
Guests wait in ride queues and leave long lines unhappy.
Handymen sweep, empty bins, and mow; mechanics fix rides; security guards prevent vandalism; entertainers cheer guests.
Paid research unlocks new rides and improvements over time.
Land can be raised and lowered and water added to fit rides and add appeal.
Coaster track is built piece by piece on the tile grid by direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews, and the result is rated by test run.
Ride reliability decays with use and age; breakdown chance rises as reliability falls, and mechanics inspect and repair on a set interval.
A Blueprint Designer (40 x 40 m at Mk.1, larger tiers in 1.0) saves layouts that appear as build-menu entries and draw materials from storage or inventory.
Refinery recipes emit heavy oil residue or polymer resin that must be routed or the line backs up, and nuclear plants emit waste that has to be stored or reprocessed.
Six belt tiers carry 60, 120, 270, 480, 780, and 1,200 items per minute, with splitters, mergers, lifts, and smart splitters routing flows in 3D.
The pioneer walks, jetpacks, ziplines, and drives across a hand-built map, building only within reach and gathering power slugs, hard drives, and samples on foot.
Pipelines carry 300 or 600 m3 per minute; liquids need head lift supplied by pumps, while gases do not.
Foundations, walls, and ramps snap to a grid at any height, so factories are stacked floors connected by belt lifts and pipes.
Early parts are crafted at a craft bench by holding a button, and equipment is made at the equipment workshop.
Clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine; each of up to three Power Shards raises the cap by 50 points, and power scales with exponent about 1.32, so 250% draws about 336% of base power.

The Space Elevator takes five Project Assembly phases of crafted parts, from 50 Smart Plating in phase 1 to Nuclear Pasta and Ballistic Warp Drives in phase 5, and its phases unlock tiers 3 to 9 and the ending.
The community-run Satisfactory Mod Loader adds new buildings, recipes, and logic on top of the Unreal Engine game.
Generators from 30 MW biomass burners to 2,500 MW nuclear plants feed one grid; if consumption exceeds production with storage empty, the fuse trips and all connected buildings stop until reset.

Smelters, constructors, assemblers, manufacturers, refineries, and blenders run per-minute recipes; 106 alternate recipes chosen from hard-drive scans swap inputs, and clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine.
Trucks and tractors replay a route the player records by driving it once, stopping at truck stations along the recorded path.
Block and path signals divide track so several trains can share a network.
Miners Mk.1 to Mk.3 sit on infinite ore nodes whose purity multiplies output by 0.5, 1, or 2; water extractors, oil extractors, and resource well pressurizers tap fluids.
Storage containers, fluid buffers, and industrial tanks buffer production; the Dimensional Depot uploads items for remote building.
HUB milestones are unlocked by delivering crafted parts tier by tier, Space Elevator phases gate tiers 3 to 9, and the MAM researches alien items, power slugs, and hard drives.
Trains follow station timetables, trucks and tractors replay recorded routes, and drones shuttle between a home port and one linked port on battery or packaged fuel.
Police pressure grows with operations through patrols, random searches, roadblocks, and night curfews; being seen raises a wanted status that can end in arrest.
Plants are grown in pots with soil and water over a growth timer, then harvested as the base product.
Customers have preferred effects and price tolerances; matching them builds repeat orders and relationships that open further customers.
A daily clock with a night curfew shapes when deals can be made.
The player personally grows, cooks, mixes, and delivers in first person until staff take over.
Grow tents, stations, and storage are placed inside bought properties.
Rank and story progress unlock new regions, customers, and equipment.
Mixing ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a base product adds named effects that raise its value and match customer preferences.
Higher products need multi-step chains such as cooking methamphetamine at chemistry stations.
Product quality varies with inputs such as soil and additives and affects price.
Dealers sell to their own customer lists for a cut, and botanists, cooks, and janitors run production at owned properties.
Movement costs are 1 on roads, 2 on plains, and 10 on swamps, and route searches consume the player's CPU, so caching paths is a core optimization.

Each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock), unused CPU banks in a bucket of up to 10,000, a tick may burst to 500, and scripts are terminated at the limit, so pathfinding and caching strategies are shaped by CPU cost.
Every creep dies after 1,500 ticks, so code must schedule replacements before roles go unfilled.
The open-source private server supports mods and community servers that change rules and tick rates.

Code spawns creeps from up to 50 body parts of eight types; part counts set harvest, carry, attack, and heal rates, MOVE parts offset fatigue of 1, 2, or 10 per part on road, plain, or swamp, and each part has 100 hits.
Official shards run continuously with ticks every 2 to 5 seconds, so colonies harvest, build, and fight while their owners are offline; rooms link through exits and shards through portals.
Terminals post public buy and sell orders priced in credits with a 5% order fee; the party executing a deal pays an energy cost that grows with distance, and NPC terminals sit at highway crossroads.

Players write JavaScript (or C, C++, Rust, Go, C#, and others via WebAssembly) whose main loop runs every tick under a per-tick CPU limit with a 10,000-unit bucket; globals reset between ticks and actions resolve together at tick end.
Towers, ramparts, and walls defend rooms against other players and NPC invaders, and a newly placed first spawn grants safe mode.
WORK parts harvest energy from sources that refill every 300 ticks, and extractors at RCL 6 mine minerals for labs and the market.

Energy spent on a room controller raises its level from 1 to 8 at cumulative costs up to 10.9 million, unlocking spawns, extensions, towers, storage, links, labs, terminal, factory, observer, and nuker; unfed controllers downgrade and become neutral.
Roads and other structures lose hits over time and must be repaired by creeps.
The player sets tank heat, cleans dirty water, and supplies food, and later runs a sprinkler to keep Frogmen moist.
Vocabulary grows through conversation, and the creature becomes tamer over time.
Tank temperature and water cleanliness must suit the current life stage.
Mushroomer, Gillman, Podfish, Tadman, and Frogman stages; Podfish parents die after mating and the aquarium becomes a terrarium.
It remembers facts the player shares, such as a birthday, and later tells historical events from that date.
Microphone speech is matched against the creature's current vocabulary; it asks for the player's birthday and other details and answers in conversation.
A neglected creature dies permanently.
Time follows the real calendar; going much longer than a day without a check can kill the creature.
Creators keep copyright to their content and sell it to other residents.
Objects are built from linked primitives, up to 256 per linked set, or from imported mesh.
The world is a grid of 256 by 256 meter regions, each simulated on a dedicated CPU core with Havok physics and capped at 40 avatars on the mainland or 100 on private islands.
Residents trade land, goods, and services for Linden Dollars, which are bought and sold for real currency on the LindeX exchange; the Marketplace has listed about 2.1 million items.
Groups give residents shared chat and voice channels.
Objects run Linden Scripting Language scripts on Linden Lab's servers, which is how built objects become interactive.
Copying and pasting factory sections costs Blueprint Points earned from goals, making repeated modules the intended way to scale.
Belts, splitters, mergers, and lifts move shapes across three building levels per platform, and space belts carry them between platforms.
Pipes and space pipes carry fluids such as paint from asteroid pumps to painters, and fluid launchers move them across notches.
Space platforms in 20x20 chunks are the limited building surface, capped by Platform Units, with notches at chunk edges as the only connection points between platforms.
After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines at the Vortex demand shapes in quantities that grow exponentially per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), absorbing late-game output.
Mods load natively through the ShapezShifter API and are distributed on Steam Workshop.
Cutters, rotators, stackers, swappers, painters, pin pushers, and crystal generators each transform shapes by fixed rules; a target shape code implies a processing sequence the player must lay out.
Asteroid miners and pumps on platforms extract raw shape fields and fluid deposits from a procedurally generated world.
Wire machines carry signals that read and control machines, and wireless senders and receivers pass signals across platform notches.

Delivering each milestone's required shapes to the Vortex unlocks the next buildings and mechanics, such as fluids, painting, crystals, and trains; afterwards, operator goal lines with exponentially rising shape costs reward platform units, blueprint points, and research points.

Space trains load fixed-size packages at loader stations and unload at stops; each rail carries trains of several colors that take their own color's branch at splitters, and wagons hold one package per machine level.
Each platform has three stacked building levels, and shapes carry up to four or five vertical layers that must be supported from below.
Crew members carry rank, experience, morale, and decorations between patrols.
A career begins at the rank of Lieutenant, Jr., with a U-boat base assignment between 1939 and 1943.
With manual targeting off, a Weapons Officer computes the firing solution.
The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in assigned patrol grids, and the player chooses targets and approaches.
Manual targeting requires identifying a vessel's class and nationality and computing its speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle before setting torpedo depth and spread.
Torpedoes run at a set speed, depth, and gyro angle toward an intercept computed from target speed and angle on the bow, so a bad solution misses.
The player is one yellow ant that digs, carries food and pebbles, receives food by trophallaxis, and fights; double-clicking another ant moves control to it.
The queen lays eggs that become larvae and adults; young queens and drones mate to found colonies in new map squares.
The colony divides into workers (forage, dig, tend brood), soldiers (fight, eat more, cannot tend brood), the queen, and winged breeders, and the player sets the balance.
Human footsteps, lawnmowers, bug spray, and electrical outlets kill ants without warning.
The yellow ant lays trails to food or enemy nests that other black ants follow, and can recruit a group of nearby ants to follow it into fights against spiders, caterpillars, antlions, or red ants.
Surface yard play is viewed from above while nests are shown in side view underground.
Rain washes away trails and can flood nests.
Tax revenue is collected periodically from population, land value, and tax rate; police, fire, and road funding fractions scale their effects, and underfunded roads decay.
A yearly evaluation turns problem scores into a 0-1000 rating and an approval poll.
Crime per cell is 128 - land value + density minus smoothed police effect, clamped 0-250.
Map windows show land value, crime, pollution, traffic density, police and fire coverage, and population density.
Each 2x2 block's value falls with distance from the population-weighted center, rises near trees and water, and drops with pollution and high crime, clamped to 1-250.
Industry and traffic write a pollution map that depresses land value and can summon the monster.
Zones must connect to coal or nuclear plants through power lines or adjacent zones; unpowered zones do not grow and lower the city score.
Fire, flood, tornado, earthquake, and a pollution-gated monster fire at 1/481, 1/241, or 1/61 per cycle by difficulty.
Three valves move by the ratio of projected to actual residents, commerce, and industry plus a tax offset, clamped to +/-2000 or +/-1500 (Micropolis source).
Time-limited scenarios such as Detroit 1972 set a goal to reach before the clock ends, added at Broderbund's suggestion.
Police and fire stations write funding-scaled effect values to a block map that is smoothed outward.
One city-wide tax rate adds a positive offset to demand at low rates and a negative offset at high rates.
Zones generate trips along roads; the resulting traffic density map adds to pollution and complaints.
The player paints 3x3 residential, commercial, and industrial zones; simulated developers build, densify, or abandon them.
Yearly budget with department funding; extreme deficit spending ends the game.
Power plant types such as solar, fusion, and microwave and buildings such as arcologies become available in set invention years as the city's calendar advances.
Water from pumps travels through underground pipes to zones.
Query tool shows land value per tile, which shapes development.
The player issues bonds to raise capital and pays interest on them.
City ordinances enacted for ongoing cost and effect.
Nine plant types including wind, hydro, solar, fusion, and microwave; most have limited lifespans and must be rebuilt.
Disasters strike in play, and scenarios based on real cities stage specific ones.
Demand bars for residential, commercial, and industrial land, raised by connections to neighbor cities.
Schools, libraries, museums, hospitals, police, and fire stations cover surrounding zones.
Separate tax rates for residential, commercial, and industrial zones.
Land has elevation that the player can raise or lower before and during play.
Query tool reports traffic on roads; highways and transit relieve it.
An underground layer holds water pipes, subways, and road tunnels separate from the surface.
Residential, commercial, and industrial zones in light and dense variants, plus seaport and airport zones.
Sims go to the first job and first empty home they find; vehicles take the shortest route rather than the one with spare capacity.
Cities in a region connect by highway, rail, and water, trade resources, share services, and pool wealth into Great Works such as an arcology.
Map resources are mostly finite, though groundwater recharges.
Water and sewage move as units through pipes between pumps, treatment, and buildings.
Pollution and traffic cross city borders within a region.
Residents and businesses come in wealth levels with different demands.
Power is carried as resource units from plants to buildings.
Service buildings dispatch vehicle agents to calls.
A simulated global market raises and lowers prices of key resources with supply and demand.
Jams emerge from masses of commuting Sim agents on the road network.
Residential, commercial, and industrial zones are painted along roads; buildings develop inside them.
Mayor mode advisors comment on problems and suggest actions.
Civic buildings need ongoing funding set per building.
Desirability is computed separately for each wealth level, so the same lot attracts different classes as services and nuisances change.
City ordinances with monthly costs and effects.
Industry and traffic pollute and reduce desirability.
Buildings belong to wealth levels and size stages; areas decay or gentrify.
Bus, subway, and rail stations carry commuters; Rush Hour adds elevated rail.
God mode triggers disasters on the city.
Demand is reported separately for each wealth level of residents and for commercial and industrial subtypes.
Schools, hospitals, police, and fire buildings cover areas; they lose output and gain maintenance cost as they age.
Tax rates per zone type and wealth level.
God mode reshapes terrain; most terraforming locks once a city is founded.
Commuters route trips over roads, rail, and transit; Rush Hour adds traffic flow tracing, avenues, and elevated rail.
Residential, commercial, and industrial zones at low, medium, and high density, with agriculture as a separate industrial zone; buildings need road frontage.
Placing terrain, life, monoliths, oxygen generators, and terraforming devices costs energy (50 per terrain square, 500 per device) from a budget that grows with planetary development.

Taxa from prokaryotes to mammals spread and diversify by environment, with player-set reproduction and mutation rates; mass extinctions are often followed by renewed radiation, and any multicellular taxon can become sapient.

Atmospheric composition, temperature, ocean level, and biomes evolve together under Gaian feedback; volcanic dust cools, warming melts ice caps, extreme heat boils oceans, and Daisyworld reduces it to daisies regulating temperature.
Hurricanes, wildfires, earthquakes, tsunamis, and meteors occur, with disease and pollution scaling with population.
Mars, Venus, Ice Planet, and Dune scenarios ask the player to make hostile planets habitable.
Designed ecosystems pair plant species with the animals that eat them, so gene edits ripple through who can feed on whom.
Evolution is simulated and can be steered; species whose genes fit the designed environment persist while others decline.
Players create and modify worlds and environments as well as species.
The player edits the genetics of plant and animal species directly, and offspring inherit those genes with variation.
People route between floors by elevators, escalators, and stairs.
Rent and sales income fund construction.
Office workers, residents, shoppers, and hotel guests travel at different times of day, creating rush periods at lobbies.
Floors and tenant units are placed on a side-view grid; tenant type and position set elevator demand.
Population and conditions advance the tower from one to five stars and then to Tower status, each step unlocking facility types.
Terrorist bomb threats with a ransom or search, fires, and pest infestations.
Tenants wait at elevator lobbies; long waits raise stress, and stressed tenants move out.
Up to 100 floors above ground and 9 below; standard elevators span 30 floors, express elevators the full height.
Missions deliver cargo or complete construction and repair jobs; optional timed contests pay more the faster they are finished.
Mechanical upgrades require reaching a progress threshold.
Mud, snow, and water react to each truck's weight, speed, and momentum, so ground conditions change as vehicles pass and can bog down underpowered or wrongly fitted trucks.
Tire types, frame attachments, and accessories such as exhaust snorkels for deep water and chain tires for snow change how each of over 60 trucks copes with terrain.
Damage is shown on the vehicle model and in the interface and must be repaired.
Tens of thousands of agents path through streets to work and services.
Alliances, trade, and war with other kingdoms.
Each citizen's needs and desires drive behavior.
Citizens and slaves of several races, each with distinct needs, religion, and roles.
Appointed nobles may try to usurp the ruler.
Every soldier must be supplied.
Real-time battles of up to 50,000 individual units commanded by the player.
Grids save as blueprints that a projector block displays for welding and that are shared on Steam Workshop.
Conveyor blocks connect inventories so refineries, assemblers, and cargo containers move items automatically, with sorters filtering flow.
Air vents pressurize sealed rooms with oxygen; breaches depressurize them.
A C# modding API, Workshop, and mod.io support custom blocks and logic.
Ships and stations are small or large grids of armor and functional blocks; thrusters only push along their facing, so thrust coverage on each axis, gyroscope count, and power supply decide handling.
The programmable block runs player-written C# scripts that read and command blocks on the grid.
Reactors, solar panels, batteries, and hydrogen engines feed every functional block on a grid; unpowered blocks stop.
Refineries turn ore into ingots and assemblers turn ingots into components for welding.
Hand drills and ship drills mine ore from voxel deposits.
Volumetric physics gives every block mass and inertia; ships drift under Newtonian motion with optional inertia dampeners, and gravity generators and planets pull loose objects.
Sensors, timer blocks, and event controllers trigger block actions without code.
Each block has hit points, and damaged functional blocks such as thrusters, reactors, and gyroscopes stop working until welded back.
In survival the suit tracks health, energy, oxygen, and hydrogen.
Asteroid and planet voxels can be drilled and carved, and armor blocks deform or break block by block under collisions and weapon fire.
Fire and smoke spread through damaged compartments.
Each tile holds gas quantities; life support modules produce oxygen and remove CO2, and hazardous gases from facilities, fires, or explosions spread until scrubbed or vented.
Hull, walls, doors, and facilities are placed freely tile by tile to form the ship, which can be expanded or rebuilt at any time.
Thermal regulators keep compartments at comfortable temperatures.
Neglected crew suffer mental breaks ranging from starting fights to venting other crew into space.
Crew needs for food, sleep, comfort, safety, and friends drive mood, alongside conditions such as starvation or feeling unhygienic.
Power nodes distribute electricity across the ship.
Each playthrough generates a new galaxy of sectors, stations, and ships.
Raw materials are refined into building materials.
Crew relationships added in 2022.
Standing with pirates, slavers, merchants, cults, and android factions.
Asteroids are mined for raw materials.
Crew are drafted and equipped for ground combat and away missions.
After completion the player's cycles, reactors, and instructions are plotted on global histograms of other players' solutions, chosen over a ranked leaderboard to avoid discouraging players.
ResearchNet distributes user-made puzzles that other players download and solve.
A solution passes when it outputs the required molecule quota and is then scored on cycles, number of reactors, and number of instructions used.

Two waldos per reactor, red and blue, follow player-placed paths and instruction icons that pick up, rotate, drop, bond, and route atoms, programmed independently or synchronized, with deterministic and visible execution.

Reactors placed on a larger planet map pass molecules through pipelines, so later puzzles split a synthesis across several reactors, some limited to tasks such as breaking bonds, with fission and fusion nodes.
Each puzzle fixes inputs, target outputs, available reactor types, and quotas; defense levels add a time pressure from an attacking enemy.
Creature inspection shows each individual's DNA and stats.
The player triggers ice ages and world floods, programs rovers to feed or kill creatures by genetic distance to a target genome, and edits genomes in an isolated nursery.
Climate varies across the map, and climate control devices create local cold, hot, fertile, or dead ground.
No fitness score exists; creatures that cannot pay skeleton-derived energy costs, reach food, or tolerate local climate fail to reproduce, so trait averages drift and lineages speciate.
Species averages over time, a clade diagram (Tree of Life), a satellite range map, and a web-of-life view of genetic variety.

Each creature's body and behavior come from numeric genes; offspring are randomly modified copies of one or more parents, with most mutations a random value in [-1, 1] times a modifier for background mutation rate and radiation.
Every creation uploads automatically to the Sporepedia and is redistributed to populate other players' worlds, so other players' designs fill the galaxy without manual import.
The player directly steers the cell, the creature, and later a spaceship.
Creature-stage species, tribes, nations, and space empires such as the Grox can be befriended through social actions or conquered.

Each stage ends at a progress threshold and hands the species to a new rule set (cell, creature, tribal, civilization, space), with three consequence traits awarded from how aggressive or social the player was.

Creature, building, and vehicle editors assemble parts such as mouths, legs, and arms whose choice sets abilities, diet options, and stats; textures and animation are applied procedurally to the assembled topology.
In the space stage rocky planets can be terraformed, their ecosystems changed, and features such as mountains and lakes added.
Tribal and civilization stages switch to commanding up to 12 tribe members, then vehicles and cities.
Farming, foraging, fishing, mining, and combat levels rise with practice and unlock recipes and professions.
Barns and coops house animals that produce eggs, milk, and wool when fed and cared for; animals cannot be slaughtered.
Community Center bundles ask for sets of crops, forage, fish, and artisan goods; completed rooms repair town infrastructure and unlock areas, and the museum collects minerals and artifacts.
Seasonal seeds need daily watering (rain or sprinklers substitute) and grow through stages over set day counts; most crops must be harvested before the season changes.
An energy bar refills each morning, drains with tool use, and is restored by food; the clock forces bed by 2 a.m. or the player passes out and loses money.
Villagers follow routines that vary by weekday, season, and weather.
Recipes turn gathered materials into sprinklers, fences, machines, and bombs.
Kegs, preserves jars, and other machines convert crops and animal products into higher-value artisan goods over fixed processing times.
