Crops and animal products come in normal, silver, gold, and iridium quality.

Each villager has a friendship stock of 250 points per heart up to 10 hearts; it decays 2 points per day without talking, takes two gifts a week, multiplies birthday gifts by 8, and unlocks heart events.
Twelve marriage candidates regardless of player gender; spouses help with chores, and couples can have children.
Four 28-day seasons gate which crops grow, which fish and forage appear, and which festivals occur.
A help-wanted board posts item, fishing, and slaying requests from townspeople.
Rain waters crops and changes fish and villager routines.
Hydroponic plants need light, water, and suitable gases, and exchange carbon dioxide for oxygen.

Rooms and pipe networks hold mixtures of oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, volatiles, pollutants, and water with pressure and temperature; gases mix, and combustion consumes fuel and oxygen and releases heat.
Pipes, pumps, filtration units, mixers, and regulators route gases between devices; pipes and tanks fail when pressure exceeds their rating.
Frames, walls, pipes, and devices are placed on a grid piece by piece, and placement decides airtightness.
Gas temperature changes pressure and habitability; radiators, heat exchangers, heaters, and coolers move heat between pipes, rooms, and the planet's atmosphere.
IC10 chips run player-written assembly that reads and writes device logic values such as pressure and temperature.
Solar panels, generators, and batteries feed cable networks; overloaded cables burn out.
Furnaces and arc furnaces smelt ore into ingots, and autolathes and other fabricators turn ingots into kits.
Ore is mined from deformable voxel terrain.
Logic readers, writers, memory, and sensors chain devices without code.
Walls hold limited pressure differences; exceeding them causes fatigue and explosive decompression.
Early survival requires breathable gas, food, water, and suit temperature; suits carry tanks and filters until a habitat is sealed.
Empire size grows with systems, colonies, and pops, and size beyond administrative capacity raises technology and tradition costs; bureaucrat jobs add capacity to offset it.
Each pop holds an ethic that drifts toward ethics with higher attraction, modified by government ethics, policies, and living conditions, and pop ethics decide faction membership.
Planets beyond the core limit can be grouped into sectors run by AI governors with a player-set focus.
Empires negotiate, form federations, and go to war; ethics such as xenophobe or xenophile shape AI attitudes.
Pops join political factions according to ethics, and faction support produces unity.
Ships are designed from hull sections and components.
Species traits and leader traits modify output and behavior.
Ethics, civics, policies, and edicts change empire rules.
Unity, produced partly by faction support, buys traditions, and influence pays for new outposts and territorial claims.

Pops fill jobs created by planetary districts and buildings in worker, specialist, and ruler strata; each job consumes and produces resources such as energy, minerals, food, consumer goods, and alloys.
Each galaxy is generated with star systems linked only by hyperlanes.
Fleet battles resolve from ship weapons, shields, armor, and hull values against each other, and ground combat compares army attack and health.

Physics, society, and engineering research each offer three semi-random project cards weighted by ethics, the scientist's traits, and known technologies; rare technologies and anomaly-granted cards vary each run, and costs rise as the game goes on.
Empires take systems by building outposts, borders follow owned systems, and claims bought with influence set what wars can take.
Anomalies found by science ships open authored event chains, and galactic crises such as marauder invasions, awakened machine empires, and extradimensional invaders begin after set periods.
War exhaustion rises from losses and occupation, and a side at maximum exhaustion can be forced into a status quo peace.
A day-night cycle and frequent eclipses change visibility.
Bases are assembled from placed modules.
Gathered resources are crafted into tools, base parts, and submersibles from blueprints the player has recovered.
Optional in Hardcore mode.
Bases and vehicles need energy sources.
Cooked fish spoils over time; cured fish does not.
Health, hunger, thirst, and oxygen deplete in Survival mode; oxygen limits each dive's depth and duration, Freedom mode removes hunger and thirst, and Creative removes all depleting stats.
Steam Workshop shares player-made characters and full neighborhoods.
A hosted language model (ChatGPT from OpenAI per the store page) generates each resident's reply and in-character decision in real time from its personality prompt and the conversation.
The player talks to residents with a real microphone, and the store page says responses depend on tone and strategy.
Each resident has an authored personality and behaviors that condition the model, and players can write their own.
Modes include Love Bites (split up couples at a Valentine's Day party) and Mic Drop (rap battles against characters).
The mouse moves the hand, holding the right button rotates it, the left button lowers it, and A, W, E, R, and Space each close one finger, so grasping a scalpel is itself the challenge.
Damage to the patient drives a small vital-sign model; when heart rate reaches 0 the player must charge the defibrillators.
Instruments, organs, and bones are physics objects that collide, slip, and fall, so most mistakes are physical accidents rather than authored failure states.
Procedures such as heart and kidney transplants are replayed in an operating room, a bouncing ambulance, and zero gravity.
Water and oxygen travel by pipe from extractors and producers to domes.
Drones within a hub's range carry resources, build, and maintain buildings.
Unhappy colonists may become Earthsick or rebels.
Comfort, sanity, health, and morale change with services and events.
Colonists have traits, flaws, and specializations that suit them to jobs.
Green Planet (2019) adds terraforming of atmosphere, temperature, and water.
Generators and batteries feed cable networks to domes and buildings; a dome without power, water, or oxygen cannot sustain colonists.
Dust storms, meteor storms, cold waves, and dust devils.
Metals, rare metals, concrete, and water are extracted; rare metal exports fund imports.
Drone hubs and dome services serve within a range.
Research spans physics, engineering, social, biotechnology, and robotics fields.
Mysteries run storylines such as plagues, rival corporations, AI revolts, and alien contact.
Buildings need drone maintenance to keep working.
Ministers and advisers brief the president and argue positions.
Available budget and resources are shown and drawn down by decisions.

Ministers, advisers, and family members present situations as dialogue, and multiple-choice responses on constitutional reform, economic model, security, and welfare trade off budget, alignment, and later options.
Sordland can side with the western or eastern bloc or stay neutral, and deals with its neighbor Rumburg.
Major choices set constitutional reforms and a market-driven or centrally planned economy.
Story chapters branch on recorded choices, opening or closing later scenes and deciding which ending the term reaches.
The device beeps and shows an attention icon when the pet needs care or calls for discipline.
Care quality during each life stage, such as unanswered calls, overfeeding snacks, and uncleaned droppings, selects the next form, so the same egg can grow into different adult characters.
Care actions are meal, snack, game, scold, clean, and medicine; meals are limited by fullness while snacks are not, and excess snacks cause sickness.
A nightly sleep period suspends care demands and marks age increments.
Baby, Child, Teenager, Adult, and Special stages (plus Senior in some models) each last a set number of days, with age advancing on waking; old age eventually ends its life.
Hunger and Happy meters, shown as hearts, deplete over real time and are refilled by meals, snacks, and the minigame.
Poor care, sickness, or old age kills the pet; the A and C buttons start a new egg.
The pet lives on the device clock set at hatching and sleeps nightly; time keeps passing between check-ins.
In most heists taking an alarmed target starts a 60-second timer to reach the getaway vehicle, so the route must be prepared during an unlimited setup phase.
Fire spreads across wood and other flammables and can burn targets or open routes; burning structures weaken and fall.
Materials respond differently to each tool and to fire; a fire extinguisher puts fires out.
Lua scripting, a level editor, and Steam Workshop support custom levels, tools, and modes.
Voxel chunks cut loose become dynamic bodies with mass that fall, roll, and crush; vehicles and cranes push and lift them.
40 campaign missions specify targets, optional targets, and conditions such as stealing, destroying, or collecting evidence.
Sections cut off from all supports fall, so removing pillars can drop a floor.
Levels are made of small voxels whose material sets which tools can break them; the sledgehammer breaks soft materials, the blowtorch cuts metal, and explosives remove volumes.
Each restored tile earns points, and points are the only currency for buildings and upgrades, so a map can stall if spending outruns restoration.
Buildings have placement rules: wind turbines go only on stone tiles and power toxin scrubbers, which clean soil so irrigators can green it.
Restored biomes attract deer, birds, fish, and bears.
Pumps refill dried riverbeds and tools carve new rivers.
Each map sets restoration targets before the player can recycle buildings and leave.
Tools create new rivers and some stone tiles.

Under polyculture, grass, bushes, trees, and carrots request a different companion plant on a tile within three moves, found with get_companion(); planting it multiplies yield, 5x before upgrades and doubling per upgrade.
Grass, bushes, trees, carrots, pumpkins, cactus, and sunflowers are planted, grown, and harvested by the drone, with Watering and Fertilizer unlocks that act on growth.
Leaderboards run the player's program from fixed starts until a resource target is met, repeated to at least two hours, and score the average completion time.
Every operation costs simulated ticks (arithmetic 1, a successful move() 200, a failed action 1), so optimizing means cutting drone actions more than statements.

A Python-like language stored in .py files drives the drone; every operation has a tick cost (arithmetic 1, a successful move 200, a failed action 1) that scales with the speed factor, and Megafarm adds more drones.
Harvested resources buy unlocks with prerequisites, including farm expansion, speed, loops, variables, functions, lists, dictionaries, polyculture, mazes, dinosaurs, and the leaderboard.
Freeform mode saves player-built puzzles, using any part, for others to solve.
Some parts react to others by fixed rules, such as a mouse running toward cheese.

Levels supply a limited inventory of parts such as balls, ropes, pulleys, belts, electrical generators, cats, and mice that the player places among fixed objects; parts act on each other by contact, rope, or belt.
A deterministic 2D physics engine with no random number generator moves balls, seesaws, and falling objects under level-set gravity and air pressure, so the same design always gives the same run.
Each puzzle states one simple goal, such as moving an object to a target, that must be met with only the parts provided.
Electrical generators driven by other parts power electrical devices in the contraption.
Nights are darker and colder, shaping travel and shelter.
Manufactured supplies are finite, so long runs shift from looting to hunting and crafting.
Hides, guts, and wood are crafted into clothing, tools, and arrows.
In Survival mode the save is deleted on death; a later DLC option allows up to three resurrections per save at a difficulty cost, and Misery mode always uses permadeath.
Food loses condition over time.

Warmth, fatigue, hunger, and thirst feed one condition stock; when a need is empty, condition drains per hour (warmth 20%, fatigue 1%, hunger 1%, thirst 2%), and afflictions such as hypothermia, frostbite, and dysentery drain or cap it.
Clothing and tools lose condition with use and must be repaired.
Wind, falling temperatures, and blizzards change how fast warmth drops and how far the player can travel; nights are significantly colder.
An online save browser with votes and comments distributes community builds.
Each cell holds one particle of an element such as powder, liquid, gas, or solid, which moves by local rules each frame; element types numbered 258 as of February 2025.
Fire and plasma ignite flammable elements and spread through fuel.
A coarser grid of air pressure and velocity moves particles and is pushed by explosions and fans and blocked by walls.
Particles carry temperature that conducts to neighbors; melting and boiling thresholds change states, and the heat display shows the field.
Element pairs react by rule: acid dissolves most materials, acid and base neutralize into salt water, fuels ignite, and neutrons from radioactive elements can drive chain reactions.
A Lua API adds elements and automation scripts; the source is GPLv3 on GitHub.
Sparks conduct through metals and semiconductors to power switches, logic gates, and machines built from elements.
The simulation can be paused and stepped frame by frame.
Cooking, Mechanical, Charisma, Body, Logic, and Creativity rise through objects such as bookshelves, mirrors, and chess tables, and gate promotions.
Free will is an option toggle; even with it on, bills, job hunting, exercise, and having children need commands.
Every household starts with 20,000 simoleons regardless of size; wages, bills, and purchases set the balance.
Ten career tracks with ten levels each; promotions need skill points and a minimum number of household friends, and change salary and hours.
The Room motive reflects lighting, cleanliness, and decorative value around the Sim.
Build and Buy modes freeze time while the player lays walls, floors, and objects on a square tile grid; object quality and layout set how efficiently motives can be met.
Eight motives (Hunger, Comfort, Hygiene, Bladder, Energy, Fun, Social, Room) decay at different rates; low motives drag down mood, and neglect can kill.
Sims die from neglect or accidents and leave an urn or tombstone; the household continues without them.
Twenty-five personality points are split across Neat, Outgoing, Active, Playful, and Nice, which change preferred activities and social outcomes.
Each pair holds a relationship score moved by interactions and eroding without contact; friend counts feed promotions.
Sims can become partners, marry, and have a baby by explicit command; neglected babies can be taken away by a social worker.
Each of the 150-plus base-game objects advertises motive gains (a refrigerator advertises Hunger, a bed Energy), and Sims query the lot's objects to find interactions.
Talk, joke, compliment, hug, kiss, tease, slap, and similar interactions succeed or fail on relationship, mood, and personality.
Free will scores advertised interactions against current motive levels so the most depleted motive tends to win; players can cancel queued autonomous actions.

Each Sim's aspiration (one of eight, such as Romance, Family, Knowledge, or Popularity) biases which wants and fears roll; fulfilled wants fill the aspiration meter, realized fears drain it, and an elder's remaining life depends on the meter.
Careers have ten levels (25 tracks counting expansions); promotions need skills and a number of family friends, and chance cards can reward or cost the job.
Build and Buy modes in a free 3D camera; neighborhood terrain can be imported from SimCity 4.
Seven life stages (baby, toddler, child, teen, young adult with University, adult, elder) advance on fixed day counts; a birthday cake or Grow Up interaction ages a Sim early.
Events such as a first kiss, a promotion, or a death are stored as memories that later shape wants and fears.
Eight motives (Hunger, Comfort, Bladder, Energy, Fun, Social, Hygiene, Environment) decay and push Sims toward objects; failing motives cause refusals and, at the extreme, death.
Elders die of old age and other Sims of accidents or neglect; deaths become memories for survivors.
Twenty-five points are spread over five opposed pairs (Neat/Sloppy, Outgoing/Shy, Active/Lazy, Playful/Serious, Nice/Grouchy); twelve zodiac presets give starting allocations.
Each pair holds a daily and a lifetime relationship score that move with interactions.
Sims court, marry, and try for babies; Nightlife adds turn-ons and turn-offs shown as up to three chemistry bolts.
Objects advertise motive and skill gains that autonomous Sims weigh against their current motive levels.
Children inherit eye color, hair color, facial structure, and personality from both parents through dominant and recessive genes; pregnancy lasts 3 Sim days.
Ten-level skills such as Logic, Cooking, Painting, Gardening, Writing, Guitar, Athletic, Handiness, Charisma, and Fishing feed careers and opportunities.
A Lifetime Wish is chosen at creation and short-term wishes appear from traits and events; fulfilled wishes pay Lifetime Happiness points spent on Lifetime Rewards.
Twelve base careers that branch around level 6, plus part-time jobs; a performance style (Work Hard, Take It Easy, Suck Up to Boss) trades mood against promotion speed.
Jobs and school run on fixed hours at rabbit-hole buildings, structuring each household's day.
Build and Buy modes with Create-a-Style, which recolors walls, floors, objects, and clothing with any pattern and material.
Seven life stages with an adjustable lifespan setting.
Moodlets are named, timed mood modifiers (for example Nauseous during pregnancy) whose sum sets mood, which affects performance at work and school.
Six motives (Hunger, Bladder, Energy, Social, Hygiene, Fun) decay and spawn negative moodlets when low.
Story Progression keeps households the player is not controlling aging, working, forming relationships, and moving around the open neighborhood; it can be switched off in the options.
Sims die of old age or of fire, starvation, drowning, or electrocution.
Adult Sims hold up to five traits chosen from a list, replacing the point sliders of earlier games; traits add exclusive interactions and bias autonomous choices.
Objects advertise motive, skill, and fun gains; traits bias which advertisements a Sim picks.
Conversation menus offer trait- and mood-gated interactions whose acceptance depends on relationship state.
Opportunities arrive from neighbors, community lots, and jobs, such as skill requests or overtime, and pay cash, raises, or relationship gains.
The chosen aspiration grants a bonus trait and a track of milestones whose completion earns reward traits; short-term whims, later reworked as wants and fears, appear from emotions and traits.
Free will can be toggled; with it off Sims act only on player orders except for urgent needs.
Sims, households, rooms, and lots can be saved to a personal library and placed again.
Careers require related skills, for example Cooking and Mixology for Culinary.
The Gallery uploads and downloads Sims, households, rooms, and buildings from other players inside the game.
Build mode draws walls and rooms, places premade rooms, and moves or duplicates whole rooms.
Newborn, infant, toddler, child, teen, young adult, adult, and elder; toddlers were added in 2017 and newborn and infant in 2023.
Moodlets carry an emotion type (such as Happy, Focused, Flirty, Angry, Tense, or Sad), an intensity, and a timer; the highest-weighted emotion becomes the Sim's dominant emotion.

Dominant emotions unlock emotion-specific interactions and raise gain for matching skills (Inspired for creative, Focused for mental, Energized for physical); extreme states such as Hysterical can kill.
Six needs (Hunger, Bladder, Energy, Social, Hygiene, Fun) decay and spawn negative moodlets such as Hungry or Bored when low.

Neighborhood Stories, added in a free update, advances unplayed households with events such as moves, relationships, and births, with settings that limit which households and event types it may touch.
Adults hold three traits and children and teens two, plus one bonus trait from the aspiration; traits add moodlets, autonomous behaviors, and exclusive interactions.
Separate friendship and romance bars per pair.
Objects advertise need, skill, and emotion gains, and Sims multitask, such as talking while cooking.
Social menus are filtered by emotion and traits, with emotion-specific variants of interactions.
Doctors can be trained to gain skills and specialisms.
Epidemics break out and can be covered up before a health inspector visits; failure brings fines and lost reputation.
Emergencies require curing a group of patients within a time limit for a bonus.
A GP diagnoses or refers patients to specialist diagnosis rooms; treatment starts once certainty passes a player-set threshold, and diseases are fictional, such as Bloaty Head.
Rooms are placed as blueprints with doors and windows, then furnished with required items; many rooms must be researched first.
Staff tire and need breaks under player-set break rules; patients need drinks and toilets.
Cures and deaths move a reputation that affects patient intake and level goals.
Each level sets goals for money, reputation, cures, and hospital value; negative funds or too many deaths lose the level.
Patients queue outside each room; the player can rearrange queues, and long waits push patients to leave.
Doctors, nurses, handymen, and receptionists are hired with performance stats; some rooms need doctors with specialist skills.
Research unlocks rooms, drugs, and machine improvements.
Machines such as the Inflator need handyman servicing or they explode.
Thugs appear when visitors are unhappy; security guards counter them.
Each visitor is an individual with its own personality and arrives and leaves by bus; unhappy crowds draw thugs who vandalize and attack entertainers.
Entry, ride, and shop prices plus ingredient levels such as sugar in ice cream decide what visitors buy and whether they come back.
Over thirty attractions, shops, toilets, and scenery are placed on a plot, with coasters needing laid-out track.
Visitors need food, drink, and toilets as their visit goes on.
On the full-simulation level, staff wage talks and supply negotiations are haggles; failed wage talks end in strikes and failed supply talks in lost shipments.
The park is judged against rival parks each year.
Visitors queue for rides and shops.
Entertainers, security guards, mechanics, and handymen are hired and their wages negotiated; understaffing brings litter, breakdowns, and crime.
A funding level drives research into new items, ride durability, staff efficiency, and bus capacity.
Rides wear down and explode if mechanics do not maintain them; research can make rides more durable.
Snipers confine survivors to the shelter by day for crafting, cooking, and care; at night survivors are assigned to sleep, guard, or scavenge.
Scavenging encounters and visitors at the door pose choices, such as robbing vulnerable NPCs or giving away supplies, that trade material gain against mood and each survivor's ending.
Radio broadcasts give weather warnings, economic updates, and war news.
Workshops craft weapons, alcohol, beds, stoves, and shelter upgrades from scavenged materials.

Mood falls with hunger, illness, loss of companions, and morally weighted acts such as stealing or killing; depressed or broken survivors refuse tasks and may leave the shelter or take their own lives.
Each survivor tracks hunger, fatigue, health, and mood, and the player must keep them up until the ceasefire.
Each survivor has one or two traits, such as Good Cook, plus hidden stats.
Winter raises demand for heating fuel.
Noisy actions while scavenging at night, such as breaking through obstacles, can alert people at the location.
Barter values change with conditions announced on the radio.
Neighbors and strangers arrive with requests tied to the shelter's state.
Recurring droughts switch sources off and badtides release contaminating badwater; both grow harsher over time and are signalled in advance.
Crops grow only on irrigated soil and fail when it dries.
Tiles exchange water through virtual pipes with evaporation; moisture spreads to nearby land and falls off sharply uphill; dams, levees, floodgates, and canals redirect flow.
Beavers need food, water, rest, and wellbeing from diet variety, entertainment, and decorations.
Water wheels and other generators power workshops and bots through a connected network.
Sensors, relays, and counters control dams and factories.
Water tanks and warehouses buffer droughts.
Explosives dig tunnels and reshape terrain.
Lodges and workshops stack on platforms; ziplines and tubeways move beavers between levels.
Strokes are drawn freely without a grid.
Walls, paths, and building outlines are turned into detailed geometry; a path through a building creates a door and raising a building adds supporting columns and beams.
Terrain height can be changed and rivers and ponds added.
StreetPass sends grown children to other players' islands.
Miis can be imported from Mii Maker or by scanning QR codes.
Adding Miis and completing objectives unlocks shops, an amusement park, a concert hall, a café, and other venues.
Each Mii receives a personality at creation that shapes its behavior.
Island time follows the 3DS clock; at night the player can listen to sleeping Miis' dreams.
Miis form friendships and conflicts on their own; pairs can grow closer, fall into fights, or break up, and the player intervenes only indirectly.
Opposite-gender friends of similar age may develop crushes; the player approves the confession, couples can marry and have a child who later moves in or leaves via StreetPass.
Miis raise problems such as wanting a food or outfit, needing relationship advice, or asking for a minigame; solving them raises happiness and pays money.
Colored blocks are added or removed anywhere on the grid, stacked vertically.
Each block edit reruns a marching-cubes-style module lookup and a wave function collapse over affected cells, then adds windows, chimneys, and bushes; delay grows with structure size.
Enclosed areas are detected and filled with gardens rather than paving.
Towns offer subsidies for serving specific routes.
Road, rail, sea, and air models are introduced on a timeline from 1930 to 2030 (1950 to 2050 in Deluxe), new models carry reliability risk, and aging fleets must be renewed as better models arrive.
Revenue per delivery depends on cargo type, quantity, distance, and transit time; mail and passengers lose value quickly while coal tolerates long, slow hauls.
Some resource sites run out and new ones appear.
Deluxe adds trading company shares and buying out competitors.
The company starts with an interest-bearing loan.
Primary industries feed secondary ones and finished goods go to towns; poorly served industries can close.
Bi-directional signals in the original; Deluxe adds one-way signals.
Local Authority ratings per town fall with poor service and tree clearing and can block demolition and new stations.
Up to seven AI transport companies compete for the same towns and industries.
Road vehicles use town roads and player-built roads from depots.
Stations accept and supply cargo only within a catchment around them, and station ratings set how much nearby industries hand over.
Rail track, including slopes, bridges, and tunnels, is laid piece by piece on the isometric tile map, with costs for terrain changes and demolition.
Trains, road vehicles, ships, aircraft, and helicopters run order lists between stations; revenue depends on cargo type, distance, quantity, and delivery time.
Vehicle reliability falls with age, breakdowns become more frequent, and vehicles must be serviced and eventually replaced; prototypes offer better specs with reliability risk.
Each citizen's happiness across categories such as food, housing, and liberty aggregates into approval.
Skilled jobs require citizens with high school or college education.
Elections can be held or rigged; losing one removes El Presidente and ends the game.
Relations with foreign powers affect trade and aid.
Buildings placed freely across the islands; bridges connect islands from the World Wars era.
Political factions each approve or disapprove of El Presidente based on conditions and decisions that match their ideology.
Edicts with costs and effects on factions and citizens.
Low approval breeds rebels, protests, and coup attempts.
Exports through docks fund the treasury.
Assistants in the marketing room run paid campaigns that draw more patients, optionally targeted at specific illnesses.
Staff earn qualifications in the training room that unlock or improve tasks.
Later levels bring epidemics with a limited vaccine supply; immunizing every infected patient earns a reward.
Steam Workshop support added in 2019.
Room prestige depends on size and decoration and affects staff happiness.
Patients start in a GP's Office and move through further diagnostic rooms until diagnosed, then to a treatment room; illnesses are comic, such as Light-Headedness and Mock Star.
Rooms are drawn and furnished with required machines, plus corridors with toilets, cafes, vending machines, and staff rooms.
Kudosh from challenges unlocks items; one star unlocks the next hospital.
Patients and staff need toilets, food, drinks, and rest.
Staff traits change efficiency and behavior.
Each hospital has star objectives; extra objectives raise the rating to two or three stars.
Patients queue at rooms while their health falls; untreated patients die, and long waits lower satisfaction.
Doctors, nurses, janitors, and assistants come with personality traits and specialisations that change performance; wages and morale must be managed.
The Research room unlocks new rooms and machine upgrades.
Machines degrade and need janitor maintenance.
Progression is skill-based with no levels or classes; skills improve as the character uses them, so a character's abilities record what the player has practiced.
Players place houses on open land in the shared world.
The economy is craft-based: players gather materials and craft the weapons, armor, and goods other players buy.
A dead character leaves a corpse that other players can loot; item insurance, added in 2003, keeps chosen items for a fee.
Shards keep persistent player houses and goods; unrestricted PvP at launch was split in 2000 into a consensual-PvP Trammel facet and an open-PvP Felucca facet.
Player guilds such as Shadowclan formed persistent communities.
The 2000 Renaissance expansion split the world into Trammel, where player-versus-player combat is consensual, and Felucca, where it is open.
Criminal acts against other players carry consequences whose rules changed over the game's life.
Player-made simulations are shared on Steam Workshop.
Orbit trails and surface temperature maps expose state that is otherwise invisible.
Collisions and stellar irradiance heat bodies, shown as molten surfaces and temperature maps.
Newtonian n-body gravity acts between all bodies; the player edits mass, density, radius, and velocity and watches orbits, ejections, spin-apart breakup, and collisions follow.
Surface temperature, sea ice, and oceans respond to stellar distance and axial tilt; moving a planet can freeze or boil it.
Planets are composed from materials such as water, rock, iron, and gases, and oceans and mountains can be shaped.
Simulation speed runs from real time to years per second and can be paused; larger time steps trade against accuracy, so fast runs can diverge from slow ones.
Gold bars are the single currency for all construction.
Points depend on population and how well it is housed, fed, and kept happy; neglect lowers the score and invites rebellion.
Each player places houses, schools, factories, hospitals, and forts on tiles of their own island, paid for with gold bars.
Rounds last 30 to 120 seconds for up to 50 rounds; factory output pays out and the score updates at each round's end.
Fishing boats earn income only while positioned over a moving school of fish.
Rebels reduce the score and can destroy buildings; a rival can pay gold to fund rebels on the other island.
Players steer fishing boats and PT boats directly; PT boats sink the opponent's fishing boat.
Randomly generated rain clouds earn income when they pass over a player's farms; tropical storms and hurricanes also occur.
Skills rise to level 100 through use and affect damage and stamina drain; dying reduces skill levels.
Some animals can be tamed and bred.
Comfort from nearby furnishings lengthens the Rested buff.
Workbenches, forges, and other stations craft tools, weapons, and building pieces; new materials unlock new recipes.
On death the player's equipment and inventory stay in a tombstone at the death site, and skill levels drop, so the player must travel back to recover gear.
Each boss leaves a trophy that grants a power at a central altar and opens the next tier of materials.
Each world is generated from a seed and divided into biomes (Meadows, Black Forest, Swamp, Mountains, Plains, Ocean, Mistlands, Deep North, Ashlands), each with its own resources, enemies, and boss.
Random events send enemies against bases.

Stability runs from blue (grounded) to red; it falls with horizontal and vertical distance from ground, a piece cannot exceed its support's stability, and vertical limits are 16 m for wood and stone and 24 m for core wood.
Food raises maximum health and stamina for a time instead of causing starvation; stamina drains when running or attacking.
Uncovered or submerged wood decays to 50% durability; tools lose durability.
Rain wets the player and rots exposed wood.
Fine-grained emotions on Ekman's typology record their target and cause.
Character files assign each agent desires that weight its action scoring.
Agents hold evaluations of each other on roles such as attractiveness or breeding, which actions raise or lower.
Social practices such as a dinner party or a conversation offer role-specific actions with preconditions, and most actions change how characters regard each other.
A drama manager agent can act to push an episode's authored plot.
Agents score each available action by executing it on the world state, evaluating the result against their desires, and undoing it; the best-scoring action is taken.
Nested tooltips break values into contributing modifiers, extended to battle and market calculations.

Pops carry a culture and a religion; over time pops assimilate toward primary cultures and convert toward the state religion, and citizenship and church laws decide which identities face discrimination.
Diplomatic plays present a demand, allow counter-demands, run a countdown to mobilize and gather backers, and become war if unresolved.
Pops buy goods to meet needs, and the share met sets their standard of living.

Pops' political strength, from wealth and enfranchisement, flows into interest groups such as the Devout, Industrialists, and Rural Folk; clout is each group's share of the national total, approval comes from laws and government membership, and enacting a law runs phases whose advance or stall chances depend on group endorsement.
Buildings hire pops by profession and qualification, so labor shortages throttle new industry.
Laws such as Free Trade and Laissez-Faire change economic and political rules.
Authority, influence, and bureaucracy are capacities with monthly supply and ongoing usage: decrees draw on authority and diplomatic pacts on influence.
The population is stored as pops by profession, culture, and religion in lower, middle, and upper strata, each with its own wages, needs, and political leanings.
Buildings such as mines, farms, and factories convert input goods to outputs; switchable production methods change the input mix, output, and which professions are employed.
Pops whose needs fall short become radicals, and radical interest groups can start a revolutionary movement with a revolution clock.

Each good has a base price, and the market price moves with the ratio of buy orders from consumption to sell orders from production, scaled by market access from infrastructure; prices feed back into building profitability, wages, and pops' cost of living.
Technologies such as the Atmospheric Engine unlock buildings and production methods.
States change hands through diplomatic plays and wars, and newly acquired states are incorporated over time before they count fully.
Each side's war support falls with exhaustion until one capitulates or the sides settle on the demands from the diplomatic play.

Two residents of a species that meet romance requirements perform a romance dance and a maze minigame that yields an egg; piñatas are ungendered, and candy skips romance requirements after a species' first romance.
Eggs and piñatas could be sent to other players over Xbox Live.
The journal of 60 species, each with requirements to discover, is the long-term goal structure.
Seeds sown with tools grow into flowers, vegetables, and trees that species eat or require; weeds spread and destroy vegetable rows if not removed.
Piñatavores must eat other piñatas to become residents or breed, and visiting predators eat residents to meet their own requirements.
Each of the 60 species has staged requirements (garden contents, plants, water, terrain, or having eaten a specific item) that turn an outline into a visitor and then a resident.
The shovel and other tools plough soil, dig ponds, and sculpt terrain.
Third-person martial-arts traversal and combat.
Players type or speak to NPCs and receive live generated replies, per the game's Steam AI disclosure.
An AI model generates Stella's dialogue and voiced performance in real time, constrained by safety filters, and her in-story decisions follow from what the player says.
Open-ended conversation by voice (a microphone is required for the full experience) or text over Stella's communicator, through video calls, voice messages, and texts.
The store tags the game as linear and story-rich, so generated conversation plays out inside a sequence of survival situations.
Health and happiness decide whether citizens stay; low loyalty raises crime and lowers work efficiency.
Conveyors move ores and bulk goods between facilities.
Optional complex education gates skilled jobs.
Liquids, water, and heating travel through pipes and tanks.
Citizens need food, clothing, and alcohol from shops.
Over 30 commodities are extracted, processed, and stored in staffed plants.
Buses, trams, trains, subways, ships, and planes carry citizens.
Rail signals and interchanges govern shared track.
Optional seasons raise heating demand in winter.
Flooding one market lowers returns there.
Exports and imports pass through customs houses at Eastern (rubles) and Western (dollars) borders.
Trucks, trains, ships, and aircraft are assigned to depots and routes that move goods and workers between buildings.
Blade element theory splits wings, control surfaces, and propellers into small elements and computes aerodynamic forces on each from geometry and physical parameters.
The plugin SDK lets developers read simulator data and add instruments, cockpit interfaces, and hardware support.
Plane Maker lets users define aircraft geometry and components and then fly the result in the simulator.
X-Plane 12 reworked clouds, turbulence, and atmospheric effects, and version 12.3 added a weather-radar system.
Time of day changes enemy and creature activity, and the Blood Moon respawns defeated enemies.
Link can climb almost any surface, glide, ride horses, and use runes.
Fire spreads across grass in the wind direction and produces updrafts that the paraglider can ride.
Cooking combines up to five ingredients in a pot into meals or elixirs whose effects and duration depend on the ingredients.
Region temperature and fire sources set a temperature gauge that damages the player beyond tolerance.

The chemistry engine gives objects properties such as flammable, metallic, or conductive; fire ignites wood and grass, metal attracts lightning in storms and conducts electricity, and ice melts near fire.

A modified Havok engine moves crates, boulders, and weapons; Magnesis lifts metal objects, Stasis freezes an object so stored hits launch it, and Cryonis raises ice pillars from water, giving shrines and fights unscripted solutions.
A stamina wheel limits sprinting, climbing, swimming, and gliding; hearts are health, and ambient cold and heat damage the player without matching clothing or elixirs.
Weapons, bows, and shields lose durability with use and shatter; the Master Sword recharges instead.
Rain makes surfaces too slippery to climb, and thunderstorms strike metal equipment with lightning.
Guest happiness depends on the animals on show, their happiness, buildings such as restrooms and shops, and scenery.
Scenery such as topiary, lamp posts, and benches gives a small guest happiness boost.
Fences, paths, buildings, foliage, and scenery are placed on a tile map.
Each species has preferred terrain types, foliage, rocks, shelters, toys, and companions; suitability drives happiness, and incompatible species in one exhibit kill each other.
Animals breed when content; babies grow into adults.
Animals need food, water, cleaning, and keeper attention that keepers supply on rounds.
Scenarios set targets such as a guest happiness level, exhibit suitability, animal count, or breeding a species.
Zookeepers, maintenance workers, and tour guides are hired.
In freeform mode, money spent on research unlocks animals, buildings, and scenery.
Fences decay and must be repaired by maintenance workers to prevent escapes.
